div.head: NOTES BY " MUST."
div.p: NOTES BY " MUST."

Football was the one thing lacking at Wilderspool last Saturday. The ground was in beautiful order, there was a crowd cf uLexpectedly large dimensions, the flag floated proudly on the breeze, and the old familiar faces with the old familiar grin were visible on the stand. It was a really fine opening of the season until the football commenced Then things began to get dull, and as time wore on they got worse until by 5 o'clock evelyb.dy had had enough of the 6easou 1912-13.

You see the match ended as it began—pointless. Warrington and the Rangers struggled valiantly, and with a great disphiy of energy, for the full 80 minutes but they neither of them scored a solitary point, and truth to tell, they did not offer one much encourage- ment to believe that if they had gone on ;Another SO minutes there would have been a different result. Each team was remarkably good at preventing the other from scoring, and this seemed to occupy all their resources. The defence was excel- lent, and .one could have admired and enjoyed it, if it had been relieved by some dashing raids productive if points. But the ideas of attack all round were terribly crude, and that is why the croiAd got bored —excessively bored. There won't be any- thing like such a gathering to-day.

Warrington's attack has bern teak for three seasons, despite the titanic efforts of a devoted com- mittee to improve it, and to-day it is worse than ever it has been. Fortunately the cause was never more obvious, so there is still a chance that it may be removed. The Wirepullers are being let down at half back—they are weak in other places too, hut it is poor half back play which is at the bottom of the want of scoring power. Here we are with three matches played, two lost and one drawn, and one try scored I That unique achievement stands to the credit of a forward.

The position is demonstrable without argument. What is being done? Well, as my readers krn,w, the club has secured Rushton, the ex-liarrow-Balle- Halifax half back. He has played in every mach tt,i, season, and be is improving, but will he strengthen Warrington's attack? I say No, emphatically. He is not the class of man that Warrington should have paid—well, a pretty big burn for. TI ere are better men in junior football. So lir, too, Brooks has failed to find his form. On Saturday he dropped more passes than he accepted, and the centres were s'arved. It is mite obvious that Brooks and Rushton will n t bring about the transformation which is rtquired.

Something else must be done, and to bttgin with I think the Commi tee ought to secure Buckley, the young Normanton half back, before the price goes up He is young and he shaped so well in the one trial here that Renwick and Dickinson both said he was the best half they had played behind in any of the practice games. It is an open secret that Rushton was pre- ferred at the time. Well, we have seen Rushton and the need for Buckley is greater than ever. There is no avoiding the fact that Warrington are in for a didastrou3 season unless they find half backs who can open the game out. A good threequarter line can be found when all the injured me 3 are available.

The only blight features of Situ' day's game were the brilliance of Jolley at full back, the pluck and pace of the forwards, and the promise of young Twist on the right wing. The Widnes lad ran with plenty of dash, tackled finely, and showed that he had an eye for an opening. He won his place. On the Broughton s'de also the full back took the honours. The team was as weak as Warrington on the attack. Though the halves were better the centres were worse—one of them g t a clear field once and punted into tcuch ! Forward, the Rangers had a big pull in weight, but they could never master the active Warrington six, not even whexa that six dwindled to four through injuries.

Luckily, Warrington are at home again to-day and may possibly capture the points from Salford. But I am very dubious about their chances, and luck will need to turn very considerably in Warrington's direc- tion if victory is to be attained. Waywell and Arnold are now added to the cripples and the selected thirteen is the weakest Wan-baton have fielded fir a lone time. Here it is: Jolley, full back ; Twist, Renwick,Mclntyre and Clare, threequarters ; Rushton end Brooks. half- backs; Thomas, Cheaters, Skelhorne, Tranter, Fearn- ley and Critchley, forwards.

It is a confession of weakness to re- introduce Clare. He might do worse than follow the example of Reid cf Widnes, and try his luck in the forwards. I should have given Carter the preference, or put Brooks wing with Renwick or Jolley at half, and " Mac " full back. Everything really depends on Rushton and Brooks finding their best form simultaneously to-day. Another display behind the scrum like last Saturday's and Salford will gain their first victory here since 1905. They are shaping well this season, with victories over Rochdale (away) and Widnes to their credit.
The S4lford team will be: Launce, full back ; Mesley, W Thomas,Wild and Loveluck, threequarters ; May and John, half backs ; E J Thomas, Rees, Thom Bevan, Currie and Goldsmith, forwards.

Warrington " A" started well at Broughton, but died away feebly in the end. Still there were some gratifying features of the display. Brown played a grand game at full back, and Davies (one of the Association players) was quite a success on the wing. Fits partner Welsby, was also worth further trial. Berry and Dixon were failures, and both have been given return tickets. Bevan was the best forward on the field, and cannot be kept out of the smior team long.

The 'A " team t--day to visit Salford, will be: Drown, full back ; Davies, Carter, Jordan and Povey, three-quarters ; Douglas and Daintith, half backs ; Bevan, Valentine, Brdndwood, Cooper, Gibbs and Naylor, forwards.

I see that Oldham have signed on D B. Davies, the Welsh International forward who played last season with Swinton. It has been common knowledge that he would not sign again for Swinton. We could have done with him at Wilderspool. Perhaps it is not too late to remind our Committee that Fairhurst, Swin- ton's hest half back, has not yet signed. He, also, is a player who would be an acquibitioo to the Wire- pullers. especially in view of the paucity of half backs. That be will be transferred before long is pretty obvious.

MR. URK ON TORY TACTICS. THE SHUNTING OF TARIFF REFORM. Addressing a meeting at Kirkliston, Linlithgowshire, Mr Ure said not one word was said on Tariff Reform during the Midlothian contest. The fories shunned it like the plague. They knew thet, taking it at its very best, they would have the utmost difficulty in getting out of it sufficient cash to pay even the maternity benefits under the Insurance Act. If Liberals could only keep steady heads and resolute minds they would have an opportunity some time about the autumn of 1915 of dealing I. final death blow to Tariff Reform. He despaired of a settlement of the great housing question until they bad the land question also settled.

div.head: ARMY MANCEUVRES.
div.p: THE ARMY MANCEUVRES.

The grand manmuvres began in earnest on Monday. The Red, or invading force, landed or. the Norfolk coast and marched on London. The Blue, or defending force, were entrenched near Newmarket. where the first battle took place. It is arranged that Cam- bridge shall be the heart of the operations.

Altogether. there are engaged in the operations 60,000 men, with 17,000 horses, and 327 guns. For the first time the Royal Flying Corps has made its appearance in mimic warfare. Our photo- graph shows a biplane being kauled into position.

div.head: Drawn Game at Warrington.
div.p: A Drawn Game at Warrington.

The first league match of the season at Warrington took place on Saturday. when Broughton Rangers were the visitors. Both learns were representative, Rushtoo (late of Batley) mak ng ais firs: apo,aarance at Wilders- pool in the Warrington ranks. Spectators rolled up in gratifying numbers, nuteithstanding a drizzliug rain, and wheu the teams commenced operations at 330 there would be a crowd of nearly 6,000 Ruing the rails. Teams and officials : Warrington. Jolley, bac's : Twist, Renwick, Mclntyre and Waywell, three quarter hacks ; Brookes and Rushton, halt backs ; Thomas, Site!borne, Treater, Fearnley, Arnold and Cheaters, forwards. Broughton —Danson' back ; Scott, Barnes, Harris and Tighe, threequarrer backs ; Jones and Barlow, half- backs; .1 L Clacopitt, (lorry, Hirst, Roberts, It Clam- pitt and Cheetham, forwards. Referee, Mr B Ennion, Wigan: touch judges, Messrs E J Hanneford, St Helens and J T Hayes, Leigh. The Rangers were much the heavier side wad in the early stages of the game forc-rd Warriugton back by strong forward play. Jolley was hard pressed but cleared brilliantly and then the home sextette changed the scene by dashing footwork. Denson was s ,on in trouble, but like Jolley he rose to to the occasion finely. Warrington maintained a sharp attack but Rushton's attempts to get the backs going were nullified by Brooks's fumbling. Play swung back to the Warrington end, and Jolley kept the toe at bay with some moat judicious touch-finding. Thomas and Skelhorne came through with the ball woen Warrington were hard pressed, and some lively work followed in the Rangers' quarter. The home forwar Is wheeled a pack and tried to rush the ball over, Arnold being hurt in the melee. He was carried from the field and absent for 20 minutes. Warrington were full of firht, how- ever' and Brooks broke through and passed to Wevwell. The latter beat Denson and punted to the line. He and Jones raced for the ball, and the Warrington wing wss howled over at the critical moment, sustaining such an injury to the shoulder that he had to jAn Arnold in the pavilion. With only four forwards opposed to their heavy pack, the Rangers made desperate efforts to score, but their combination was poor end Jolley, Renwick and Mclntyre set up a defence which was magnificent. Five minutes irons the interval ‘Verring- ton's two cripples limped on, but wera of Mai ties. Half-time: No score. On resuming t'le Warrington men made a fine eft )rt to take the lead. By sheer Out rmination they forced the Rangers back, and both Caesters and Skelhoroe had hard luck in not cros•ing the line. Bara.s broke away and had a glorious Chance, but when challenged by Jolley he weakly punted and the ball rolled in touch. Renwick and Mclntyre got going on the right. but a poor pass to Twist spoiled the opening. Still, the advantage was with Warrington, and better handling at the base of the pack must have brought points. Rushton made a plucky attempt to dodge over from a scrum near the line and was grassed. Broughton were penned in, and henwick got the hall out t 4 Twist, who raced over at the corner, but was recalled for a forward transfer. Finally a penalty relieved the Broughton line, and play became more even. Renwick tried a shot at goal from half-way, hut the ball fell short, and the end came with the score-board still reading 000. WIDNES UNFORTUNATE AT SALFORD.

About 5,000 people at The Willovrs,Weaste, witnessed a vigorous and exciting game,Salford defeating Widnes after a hard Wesel. No quarter was given on either side, and U e referee more than (rice extended towards some, of the players gentle caution. Widnes were penalised early on and Me..ley kicked a goal for Salford. Subsequently Swinton got over for the visitors, laylor failing at the place. 111esley secured a try for the home side, but failed at goal. flalf-time:—Sal ford 1 goal 1 try (5 points), Widnes I try (3 points). In the second half both sides attacked in turn, but at the finish Salford dominated the situation. Loveluck scored a try, and Mesley, besides adding the extra points, kicked three mote goals, two from penalties and one from a mark. Swinton and Rk ed scored tries for Widnes, and Taylor landed a goal. Result :—Salford 5 goals and 2 tries (16 points), Widnes 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points). Teams : Salford—Latmce, back ; Callender, W Thomas, Llve- luck and Mesley, three-quarter backs ; May and John, half-backs ;E J Thomas, Rees, Bevan, Thorn, Currie, and Goldsmith, forward. Referee : 111 r F Renton, Hunslet. KEEN GAME AT RUNCORN.

- - - - Helecs appeared at Runcorn on Saturday and won somewhat luckily. Before the game was five minutes old St.llelens were ahead as the result of a try obtained by Prescott, who bad a clear run through for Turtill to add the goal points. The Linnets were not long in retaliating, a passing movement sending Richardson over in fine style, and he added the goal. Browning obtained the &lints' second try after almost every man on the side had handled. At tbe interval tbe bfiltitS led by 8 points to 5. A beautiful bit of work by Moran, who intercepted a his h pass, enabled Runcorn to draw level but the Saints were soon a try up again as the result of a mistake by Pacroury on his own line. Fir al : St Helens 11 pointi, Runcorn 8 points. LOSTOCKPR A LAM V. OUGHTRINGTON AMATEURS. Lest ralatu 5, Ougiatntigton Am.t4tms 0. LATCII FORD V. ST. VINCENT'S.

At Thel wall-bine, Latchford on Saturday. Latchford were the first to score shortly before the inr.erval through a misunderstanding between RUES and Giles, Potter tetzing the opportunity and making no ! mistake. Half-time : Latchford one, St. Vincent's nil. Resuming, St. Vincent's were the first to attack, Dudley missing a tine chance of equalizing, A brilliant com- bined run by the whole of the home forwards was nullified by Giles. In the latter stages of the game Latchford took the upper hand—Potter, the home centre, being a continual source of danger to the visitors' defence, and with a shot which cannoned off Ross, added No. 2, following with a third, and thus completong the hat trick a few minutes later. No further scoring took place. Final : Latchford, 3, St. Vincents 0. BROADFIKATH V. OUGHTRINGTON PARK. At Navigation-road. Broadneath. toe visitors a-rived short-ttanded and kicked oft late. After several futile attempts Pete tck opened the score for the Heathens. Half-tide: Broadbeath 1, Oughtrington Park, O. Re- suming, tbe home team had the best of matters, but met us sound defence. Frank Thomason in particular being in good form. Before the close Coeter added a rather rimple goal for Browlheith, Simpson being at fault and allowing the hall to roll beneath his hands into the net. rinal Broadhesth 2. Oughtrington Perk nil.

div.head: SECOND DIVISION.
div.p: SECOND DIVISION.

STOCKTON HEATH v. LATCHFORD RECREATION. At Stockton Heath. Toe Rees, wore the first to score through Evats. Half-time : Latchford Recreation 1, Stockton 11>ath, nil. In the second half Stockton Heath gradually took a firmer hold on the game, their right wing being prominent. Eventuklly Dean equalized lot them, whilst close on time Craik gave them the lead and victory with the score : Stockton Heath 2, Latchford Recreation 1. PADGATE AMATEURS V LATCHFORD BRITANNIA.

ACVaiig-a-te-;;;Siu-i:day. The game began evenly. but at the end of 25 minutes the visitors opened their account. No further scoring took place before the interval, when the score was : Latchford Britannia 4, Padgate Amateurs 0. In the second portion play was more brisk and the home team equalized with a very simple shot, whilst from a penalty they took the lead a few minutes later. The Britannia rallied and improved, sue with a good eff irt equalized the scores. The closing stages of the game were keenly fought out, and shortly hafore the time the visitirs again got in front. Tae final being : Latchford Britannia 3, Padgate Amateurs 2. WEAVER REFINING ro. v. NEWTON COMMON..
Weaver Refining Co, 3, Newton Common Albion, I WIDNES ALLIANCE LEAGUE.
GHAT SANKF.Y V. FARXWORTII NAUTICAL SCHO3L

Played at Sankey on Saturday. The game was only ten minutes old when El Ray, breaking away on the left, put in a splendid centre, wnich T Cook converted. Three minutes later A Whittaker added a second with a fine shot. This put the visitors on their mettle, and taking Sankey by surprise, came within an ace of selling. J Gorman, in attempt- ing to clear a low drive from H Ray, put the ball through his own oal. The locals con- tined to press and T Cook literally walked the ball through the visiting defence and scored a fourth. The visitors replied with a flue run on the left, and J Dwyer scored with a fast cross shot. F Millington added a fifth for Sankey from 25 yards range. .1 Dwyer scored a second for the visitors. Half-time : Great Sankey, five goals ; Farnworth N.S., two goals. Resuming J Baker added a sixth, T Cook a seventh and J Baker the eighth goal for the locals. From a corner taken by .1 Dwyer, J. Mansfield headed a third for the visitors. Final : Great Sankey, eight goals ; Farnvvorth N.S , three goals. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT ALLIANCE. Sr. BARNABAS° V ORFORD WHITE STAR.

These teams met on the Lovely-lane ground. The Saints opened in sterling fashion, and the Star goal was quickly under-going a bombardment. Lawton relieved nith a good kick. At the other end Lee was prominent with a great individual effort which ended in Moody having to throw away. Afterwards play settled in the visitors half, but although eeverirl opportunities presented themselves to the home forwards, there was no score at half time. On restarting, the home team pressed. A penalty having been given against one of the Star's defenders for handling, Robinson opened the score. Shortly afterwards another penalty was awarded which was netted by Itobinson. Play was at once transferred, the home defence being in danger when a penalty was given against Helsby,from which Lee scored The Saints pulled themselves together, Millington adding the third end Challinor the fourth and fifth goals. Bates scored a second for the Star. Result : St Barnabas 5 goals, Orford White Star 2 goals.

ORFORD BARRACKS V LIEUTENANTS ATHLETIC (LIVERPOOL). The above match in the fi at round of the Liverpool Hospital Cup Competition took place on the ground of the former club on Wednesday. There was a fair attendance, principally military. The visitors were completely outplayed, and the match resulted in a runoaway victory for the soldiers of 17 goals to none. Goals were scored by \Lieutenant Doll 4, Private Trafford 6, Private Forahaw 3, Colour Sergeant Pr. ctor 1. Corporal White 1, Private Lonwen 1, Private hanky 1.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT CRICKET LEAGUE. Tt e Championship.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT CRICKET LEAGUE. Tt e Championship.

A special meeting of the League Committee was held on Wednesday at the Roan Cow Inn, Mr. J. W. Travis presiding. The chief business was the appeal of the Rylands Club against the decision of the com- mittee in respect of their match with Orford. After further discussion the committee upheld their former ruling to allow the match to stand as a draw each club being awarded one point. The Sankey club can now be termed the Champions.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
A PLEA FOR INCREASED SUPPORT.
The Coming Season's Work.

A strong plea for increased interest in the work of 'the Warrington Musical Society was made at the annual meeting which was held in Cairo-street Schools on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Sir 'Gilbert Greenall Bart., C.V.O. As the proceedings immediately followed the usual weekly rehearsal, 'there was a large attendance of members. Amongst I,hose present were Messrs. Roger C. Parr, Lionel airclough (hon. secretary), John P. Reynolds (hon. treasurer), and Frank H. Crossley (conductor).

div.head: SECRETARY'S REVIEW OF THE SEASON.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REVIEW OF THE SEASON.

In presenting his annual report, the hon. secretary referred to the very serious loss the society bad sus- tamed since the end of last season by the death of Mr. Chas. White, one of their most enthusiastic and ardent supporters, and one who had helped them in Many and various ways for about fifty years. Last season opened as usual with the opera. "San Toy" 'was the work selected and it proved a great success not only by reason of the popularity it enjoyed, but also on account of the financial return. One point he hoped Members would take to heart was that after the opera !vas over a considerable number of members taking part M it seemed to have expended all their energy upon it and were unable to attend the ordinary practices. Last season the attendance of the opera members of the ,chorous at practices was bed. The opera was not the chief aim and object of the society, and it should not be made an excuse for members to shirk the ordinary practices. The strength of the chorus last season was : --Sopranos, 71; contraltos, GO ; tenors, 22 ; basses, 34. There were 30 rehearsals, and the percentages of the •attendances was :—Altos, 58.33 ; tenors, 5454 ; sePranos, 53.42 ; and basses, 4706. The chorus was dreadfully lacking in male voices—especially tenors— and thus it was not as well balanced as it might be. THE ATTENDANCES OF THE CHORUS. Mr. CROSSLEY then gave an outline of the coming season's work. At the outset he said he was glad the Hon. Secretary had drawn attention to the irregular attendance of members last season. He had tried to impress upon the members of the opera section the importance and necessity of regular attendance at the concert rehear.als. The opera was not the first thing in the society's aims. \Wen it was considered that the opera members were also members of the whole society, their attendance at rehearsals should be better than it had heen. Apart from the opera the practices had not been well attended and towards the end of the season he circularised the members on the point. They ought really to take it to heart. Perhaps it was more carelessness than anything else. Members joining societies like that ought not to think they coulo attend as they pleased. Each member was responsible to some extent for the success of the whole undertaking. No good work could be done without adequate practice. The practices last year were only attended by half the members. He was very sorry that that should have to go to the public. A society of that character ought to be ashamed of itself if it could not do better. 'l'he attendance of the orchestra was infinitely better. He reminded them that the rules empowered the conductor to prevent any member who bad not attended the rehearsals regularly and punctually from taking part in the concert. It would be ,an unpleasant duty to have to tell anyone no to sing at a concert, and he hoped it would never fall to his lot. Better work would be done if the practices were attended more frrquently. It was proposed to give three concerts during the coming season. The dates flae 1 were November 6th, January 15th and March 12th. A fine violinist had been engaged for the first concert, and the instrumental work would consist of Tschatkowsy's violin concerto and another short work. The vocal items comprised C deridge Taylor's " Viking song," and 0 The lee shore," German's" Sleeping "sod Stanford's " Phaulrig Crohoore." For the second concert the last choral work of the late lamented Coleridge Taylor " A song of old Japan " and miscel- lanous items would be given. The March programme would consist of the first two parts of Haydn's "Creation " and a few miscellaneous works. They hat a very interesting season to look forward to musically. There would be a great deal of work to do,but those who were keen and loyal would not mind that. (Applause).

For three whole months I have been travelling through the largest country in Europe. I have passed over more than 12,000 kilometres by rail or by boat. and although I know not more than ten words of Russian, yet my travelling is always quite easy and full of pleasure. Esperanto has solved the problem, and thanks to it, in recounting my journeyings I do not, like Mons. Riviere, have to speak of the difficulties of such a voyage, but only of its ease! I am alone only between-times, oa the ship or in the train, and it is of those few hours I wish to speak. In Russia the trains are spacious and comfortable (also shockingly slow ! but people do mot mind that), and it is the custom to make oneself quite " at home" when travelling by them. So Russians always bring with them into the trains enormous packages, con- taining everything necessary to comfort. If a carriage has three or four persons in it, it is not li.ng before mutual introductions take place, and if I am one of the number, something liise the following usually happens. 1 am asked a question in Russia". I reply in Russian that I do not understand. One of the party then generally tries me again in German or French, and as I can speak a broken sentence or two in both of these languages, I give some explanation in reply to such questions : " Yon are a tourist, sir ? "
_ "Oh no, I am travelling for the Chamla>rs of Commetce of California, to make my country known abroad."

"You are merely passing through Russia ? " "1 am passing through, but not merely' for I have already given public lectures in twenty-four of its principal towns, from St. Petersburg to Tiflis, from Warsaw to Saratov "

" But you don't speak Russian "Do not even need it! " I reply. " ? ? - They hesitate, wondering vvbether to think me a madman or whether they have under- stood me aright. "What on edrth do you mean ? " Whereat I continue:

" Well, gentlemen, have you never heard of the International Language which has now been accepted as an established fact ? I use that language, and not only in Russia, but throughout Europe as well. I have already visited the capitals of twenty different countries in Europe, and of two in North Africa, and in each one of them I have given lectures in this language" And I produce my map, on which is marked a line showing my way through Europe during fifteen months' constant travelling. As I travel second class, I nearly always find, among four fellow- passengers, three who spsak French or German who are even themselves French or German or of some other nationality other than Russians. They grow interested about this possibility of travelling without knowing any language beyond one's own, and begin to ask questions about the" international language " (the name of which, by the way I have not yet told them ! ) So I begin to explain : "Xou sir, are a Russian; you a German; and you a Frenchman. You are able to understand one another more or less, for even if you do not know all of each of the languages you represent, you at least possess between you some hundreds of words which are the same in all of them. You could even by means of these words carry on a little conversation. That com- mon stock is the basis of my international language. A man of genius in your own country, sir, Russia, thought out a simple grammar, gathered together the words common to or understood by the greatest num- ber of nationalities, and having given them a phonetic spelling, printed a pamphlet in which he called the combination he had produced Lingvo Internacia.' It is known now as 'Esperanto,' and of course you have heard of Esperanto, have you not ?" Their surprise is greater than over! Of course they have heard of Esperanto, and also, either covertly, or quite openly, have derided it. "But we never thought for a moment that Esperanto was really a success." .

" Gentlemen, you, and many others, remind me of the man who saw a dromedary for the first time. After staring in perplexity at the strange—and, to him, quite new—beast, he turned away, muttering: 'Such a creature does not exist!' Can you, too, see Esperantu succeeding before you and still deny that it really lives? That would surely be too naive ! " I always carry with me propaganda matter in Russian, hundreds of Cefec " keys," and in words, specially chosen for their likeness to words in the languages of my listeners, I explain and give examples of the internationality of Esperanto. They read, are convinced, and believe, for who could do otherwise?

Ways are long in Russia; evening draws near, night comes —and one of my three fellow voyagers, the only Russian, extracting from his heap of luggage various objects, places them on the table, a candle (which is all the light to be had on most trains), a tea-pot, sugar, bread, and perhaps cheese, some meat, &c. At the next station he gets Some hot water and soon we shall he partaking of excellent tea, made as only Russians know how to make it ! We eat together at his kindly invitation, but in order to have the necessary glasses hive to remove them from the public water bottles at the ends of the train ! Two, three, four glasses of tea, with plenty of sugar, often with some sort of Jam, while already, in crude Esperanto, we can quite easily make ourselves under- stood one to another. When finally we part, I point out to them how in a few hours four men of diffetent nationality have managed to get along together in "crude Esperanto," and ask them whether after all it is wise to deride the man who makes use of this international language ready to his hand." " Adiau, sinjorcj ; lernu Esperanton "

MRS. JOIN CROSFIELD OPENS THE NEW VESTRY.

Ever since its f .andation by the late Mr. John Crosfield, the Woikinginen's Mission, flank Quay, has made consistent progress until t DOW exercises an incalculable influence for good iii a populous working- class neighbourhood. Further evidence of its expan- sion was fotthcoming on Saturday when the handsome and well appointed new vestry, tendered necessary by the ever increasing demands upon the Sunday School accommodation, was ovened by Mrs. John Cro-field, of Colw) /I Bay. 'rhe entire cost of the structure and furniture (about ;C,600) has been generously borne by ' Mrs. Crosfield who takes a keen practmal interest in the work of the mission', The building, which will accommodate about 140 adults, has been erec!ed by Messrs C W 1)-nvenoort and S its, Si. cktort Heath, to the design of Mr S P &Mock, F.R.I 8.A., Warning- ton. It is entirely iii harmony witn the rest of the mission premises and id ,ally adapted fir class meet- ings and many other useful purp ices to which it will be devoted. Movable pa,titions are provided, so trot the room may be divided into sections when occ isi, n arises. Tilf3 opening of the vestry v,as regarded as a red letter occasion in the history of the mission and thete was a large gathering of Sunday School workers and members of the colgregation.

div.head: iUF OVENINU CEREMONY. [Photo Barre' Mr. S P. t ilcock, Mr. Hassall, Mts. Cro:field, Mr. T. Dale, Rev. John )(cogs.
div.p: iUF OVENINU CEREMONY. [Photo Barre' Mr. S P. t ilcock, Mr. Hassall, Mts. Cro:field, Mr. T. Dale, Rev. John )(cogs.

The first pert of the proceergiags took place in the schoolroom where the 11) run Unto Irby temple Lord, we come' woe sting and Mr. G DALE offered prayer. Then the congregation walker to the entrance of it e new vestry where the brief formal opening ass enacted. Mr. S P. SILCOCK archii ect, oir behatt of the builders, asked Mrs. Crostield's acceptance of a silver key as a memento of the the occa-dou. He said that was the second occasion within is comparatively short period that he had had that pleasurable dio v to perform, the first time be.rig at the opening ot Friars' (ire Hall, and now that splendid addition to the rhea Its- street school, the whole cost of which had been so generously borne by Mrs Ciosileld. He said, on tre occasir n of the opening of Vriars' Green Hall, and he would repeat it, that the friends might have look. d Warrington over and not have found so kind and generous a lady as Mrs Cr Afield. He prayed that she might long he spored to come amongst them rind see; the fruits of her kindners end generosity. (Applause) Mrs. Citosmkto accepted the key V% biCh be said she would rilways prize as a memento of the happy occasion. In declaring the vestry open, sire expressed the hope that it would be the means of increasing the good which Was being done in that neighbourhood by the Workingmen's Mission. (Applause). The assembly then entered this vestry, where the Rev W REID, who presided, formally dedicated the building and offered prayer. Mis.CROsFikLD, in the course of a brief address, said she had realized for some time that if the work of that large and increasing Sunday school was to be satisfactorily carried on, they must have more accom- modation. She was therefore very glad to find that there was just enough room to build that addition, and it was a great pleasure and satisfaction to her to see it completed so soon. The architect and the builders deserved their heartiest congratulations upon the excellent and artistic way in which the work bad been carried out. (Hear, bear.) Having seen the extension when it was only partially completed, she was now quite surprised to find it looked very much larger than she had expected—in fact, it was a very pleasing and chorruing little hall in every respect. When she was asled by the Secieorry (Mr Tilling) a few months ago if she could suggest a name for the ball, she could not think of one. The other evening, however, she was returning from a most beautiful day's excursion in the Higlitanda—to Loch Medea. Whether it was that those wounerfril and glorious mountains and hills, clad in their deep rich purple heather.bracken and fir trees, suggested the moue to her he did not know, but that night she could think of no other word but " Excelsior." To most of them' Longfellow's fine poem would be familiar and she must say that the word, expressing "'Onward, upward, ever higher,' represented what all of them, 3 oung and old, should be striving for. 'their restless hearts could only find rest in the attainment of the eternal, when they reached the City whose Maker and Founder Was God. She was very pleased to think that the hall would be occupied on Sundays by the young men's class who certainly deserved it, for they Lad been very much crowded in the old vestry. She hoped the class would continue to prosper and that the good work which was being doze at the mission would increase more and more as the 3 eras went on. (Applause.) The Rev \V REID then read the lesson. In RD address the rev gentleman referred to the difficulties to be encountered by all who attempted work for God. There was a temper in the world—and sometimes it came very near to those who ought not to be of the world—a temper that would villify any good in which they did not happen to have a share. Tee hest protec- tion of Christian workers, under such circumstances, was their own innocence and purity of motive, the knowledge that they were not seeking their own glory, but the glory of God. The speaker also referred to the difficulties placed in the path of Christians by those who were not really the prophets of God, but hireling prophets, and by those who were actually of their own household. Whatever obstacles they bad to meet, the very fact that they were engaged in a great, noble work was the finest antidote for fesr, the finest salve for wounds, and the only t.ing they needed in the way of inspiration. " I am eugsged in a great work" should be their cry right to the end. (Applause). Councillor IdESSFIALL said be bad been associated with that cause for nearly thirty years. He remembered the day of small thing-, when the mission room was in Liverpool-road, and those who in those early d ye were staunch to the work, through good and evil report, probably never expected to see such handsome, spacious and beautiful buildings as the mission now possessed. The note he was disposed to strike was one of optimism. The late Mr John Cros- field was especially anxious that the mission should above everything else,be a workingmen's cause,monaged by workingmen, that there should pervade it through and through sense of homeliness, it consciousness of one-ness, that there should come to each of the workers not only the sense of the dignity but the high and holy privilege of serving God in serving his fellows. Those who knew the history ef the work would know that that had been its characteristic note from its small beginnings until it had reached its zenith in the com- pleted buildings they saw that day. The thought which he would emphasise was that all those buildinis were a sign and symbol of that wonderful metaphor of the Apostle wherein he reniinded them that they were builders together with God, that the foundotion was laid deep, wide and for ever. It was the privilege of those who worked at the Mission to strive to put into the fair fabric of the characters of the young people those doctrines which would be as gold, silver and costly warble, and to have the consciousness that in building char,+crer they were building for ever. There never was ft day when, amid our ceaseless and manifold activities, and with the growing tendency to woiship the material, we needed so strongly to emphasise that it was the quality of the heart and soul, that it was righteousness that exalted a man as a nation, and that sin in the unit, as in the aggregate, was a reproach to any people. Might the young people, who were the heirs of the ages and trustees or prosperity, learn at that mission self-knowledge, wisdom and self-reverence. (Applause). The Rev JOHN YONGE recalled the fact that he parti- cipated in the opening of the schools thirteen years ago. The new vestry, he continued, reflected the greatest

They lelieved Mrs. Crostleid had accurately divined the si,iritand intention of their late beloved founder (Mr. John Croifield) by eye mraging in every possible way the development of the great and growing Christian work at Batik Quay. The ittluence of the mission had sped in numherless homes and bad been of great service in the neighnourhood. Tbe attendance at the school on Sunday afternoon numbered between GOO and 700 and be believed it was the greatest work of the Lind in Warrington. He did not say that in any boasting spirit, but would lice it. to stimulate every came in Warrington in That direction. He had be.-u enpaeed in the work for forty 3 ears., and had always believed that work among the young pet pie was the best in which any Christian could pirticipate. rhey were pleased to have the presence of the father of the Free Churches in War- rington, the Rev John Yonge. (Applause). Although he had retired from the work in connection with his own church, they were delighted that he was willing to give a helping hand wherever be could, and they hoped his Ihtter years would be rich with blessing. (Applause.) The vote was heartily passed. Mrs. CRC/5.1,18U) responded arid also presented Mr Alfred Tilling (secretary of the Mission) with a copy of Tennyson's poems as a recognition of his work in connection with the undertaking Mr isILLING, in responding, said they had every reason to be proud of the new vestry wh,ch was urgently needed. If they recognised the duty of teaching to the children the great doctrines which in many instances were not being taught in the da; school they could not over-estimate the importance of Sunday school work, lie was thankful they had associated with them at that mission a leader like Mrs Crostield and that they could also count upon the simport of the Crisfield family in any scheme for extending the work of God in the Bans Qusy district. (Applause.)

It was out of this condition that Mrs. Alice E. Dry, of 15, Prospect Terrace, York, was brought back to health by Dr. Cassell's Tablets. Here is her story : lor four years," she says " I suffered misery from indigestion and kidney tiouble. I felt ill all over me, with dreadful pains in my stomach and across my back. I had DO appetite, and what I did eat just turned to wind, and added to my suffeting. div.head: SUNSHINE IN THE WEST.
div.p: SUNSHINE IN THE WEST.

It is remarkable that despite the advance of the season, maximum sunshine is being experienced at the Cornish and West of England seaside resorts generally, and exceptionally fine weather is reported at Falmouth, Penzance, Newqnay, Torquay, Weston-super-Mare and Weymouth. Many who deteried their holidays owing to the uncongenial weather last month and have gone to the West owing to the lateness of the sear, are now enloSing their bolidas a under ideal conditions.

Our avocations, widely different as they were, led to a separation ; we lived miles apart, but for a few years corresponded frequently, and one of his letters (which I still possess) tells of the difficulty he had in persuading the Committee of Management of the Exhibition, and especially Lord de Tabley, its pre— sident, that a bedstead could be properly regarded as an art treasure. A sight of it, however, convinced them, and it proved an attraction.

Some five and twenty, or thirty years ago -I can- not fix the date—l was in London and visited the Royal Academy Exhibition. Whilst viewing one of the works, I received a smart blow on the shoulders, and turning round in surprise, found the miter to be my old friend. After a b-ief chat about my native town, the town of his adoption, be said. "Came with me into the next room, and I'll show ycu something:' We went together, and directing my attention to a fine portrait of himself, remarked " lon cannot guess who painted that." "No, indeed," I answered, and then he asked, "Do you remember, "hen ou lived in Warrington, a little boy that used to come to your house, almost always on Fridays ?" I replied, " I do. A bright, yet serious-minded lad, your son." " Well," he explained, with pride in his voice and manner, " he is the painter of that portrait." We adjourned to the refreshment room to talk over 'r old times, and of the success of his talented son, whom I recollected when he was quite a little fellow joining the Warrington School of Art as a student. "My boy," he said, "is at Hatfield to-day, but he will be back to-morrow, and you must come and see him." Alas! I had to return to Dewabury by a train departing in a few hours, and so lost the opportunity I should so much have enjoyed. My old friend and I parted from each other at King's Cross Railway station, and we never met again. Like his son he hats joined the great majority. This reminiscence may perhaps interest a few readers.—Yours, &c.
W. W. YATES.
Elmwood Terrace, Dewsbury. September 15th, 1912.

div.head: ART OF JAMES CHARLES AND
div.p: THE ART OF JAMES CHARLES AND
GEORGE SHEFFIELD.

In an article on the exhibition of works of four Lancashire artists at the Manchester City Art Gallery, a writer in the "Liverpool Daily Post and Mercury" thus refers to pictures by two famous Warrington artists—James Charles, a native of the town, and George Sheffield, who received part of his training and did much of his work here : One of the four rooms of which the exhibition is composed is allotted to each of the artists named. The first to Charles, the realist, who brought his trained faculties to bear on the task of discovering beauties in the common sights of daily life, and his perfectly trained hand and eye to the work of reproducing them by the medium of his art. Such painters rarely achieve the highest flights of art, but their qualities of industry and sincerity in tepre- sentation are essential to the perfect artist. To enter Mr. Charles's room is to enter a world where common

things illumined by a sweet, sane mind, become beautiful. The art of a Chad es, because it is realistic is not strongly individual; it takes its hue and shape from outer things which change, rather than from inward ideals that are constant. He goes to Italy, and his art is touched with that dazzling brightness paradoxically tinged with melancholy characteristic of the Italian landscape. as is evidenced by his " Scene in Ana—Capri "(31). Again, he stands in a blossom-bovvered English lane, and you have the unaffected simplicity of " The Little Totterer " (73), and fall a-wondering how the same hand could pro- duce the two pictures, forgetful that the mind of the realist is controlled by external things. Again, he is confronted by a broad wind-swept landscape, as in No. 42, and you imagine that he must have seen it through the eyes of Linnell, so impersonal is his art. But from whatever standpoint be approaches his subject, the result is sweet, wholesome, and good. In the third place we come to the room of Sheffield, the picture-maker. Let not the testhetes turn up their superior noses, for Sheffield also has his place in art— and a not unworthy place. The consideration which determined his choice of a subject was whether it would make a picture; and he brought to the execu- tion of his work a judgment that seldom erred and a hand trained to the highest degree of efficiency. The Art SAlool of Manchester may be proud to have pro- duced such a craftsman as George Sheffield. Like many of his fellows, Sheffield often put more into his work than he himself, perhaps, knew. We do not envy the spectator who can look at " The Empire's Frontier" (143) and " Cromwell's Monument" (165) without a glowing conviction of the greatness of our race and its achievements. If it be said that to pro- duce such impressions is not the function of art, we retort that to make the man a better citizen and the citizen a better man is a task of which the highest of high art need not be ashamed.

div.head: JAMES CHARLES AND WARRINGTON. Interesting Reminiscences. The following letter appeared in Monday's" Yorkshire Post "
div.p: JAMES CHARLES AND WARRINGTON. Interesting Reminiscences. The following letter appeared in Monday's" York- shire Post "
TO THE EDITOR.

Sir,—l was greatly interested on Saturday in the article by your Special Correspondent on the works of the four deceased Lancashire artists, about to be exhibited at the City Art Gallery, in Manchester, an institution—if I may say so in parenthesis—of which I had some knowledge seventy • years ago, and I crave a little space to say a few words about the first-named of the four—Tames Charles, of Warrington, and his father, Richard Charles, one of my most intimate companions during later youth and early manhood. Richard had strong artistic gifts which be applied in designing furniture of the highest class for Messrs. Garnett and Co., of Warrington, a firm of much more than local reputation, and I well remember that a suite shown by them at the great Exhibition in Vienna carried off a very high prize, lie possessed, also, extraordinary skill as a carver in wood, and at the Art Treasures Exhibition, held in Manchester in 1807, be displayed a bedstead that was disposed of for £7OO. It was a iemarkably fice specimen of art workmanship.

div.head: TORYISM IN TWO ASPECTS.
div.p: TORYISM IN TWO ASPECTS.

Lady DOROTHY NEVILL, that delightful old lady who in her earlier days was one of the friends of Lord BEACONSFIELD, and who wrote a few years since an ingratiating book on her own times, has now made a still further draft on her memories, and between her various anecdotes has interspersed re- flections which are interestingly character- istic of her age, temperament and position. Lady DOROTHY is, of course, a born Con- servative. Her point of view is that of the aristocratic woman of, let us say, the middle of last century, when Toryism was still Toryism, and when Sir ROBERT PEEL, according to DISRAELI'S famous description had found the •Whigs bathing and run away with their clothes. Nobody in Lady DOROTHY NEVILL'S rank of life would then have believed that they would live to see a Conservative party adapting itself to circumstances, and adopt- ing a policy in the flash of a moment, as in the case of the Referendum. In the middle of the last century some sixteen or seventeen years had to pass before the EARL OF DERBY

described the Reform Bill of his own Govern- ment as "a leap in the dark." The Tory party had no thought at that time of going forward, like Columbus, in search of a new world. It was, to all appearances, firmly anchored to its ancient faiths.

And now Lady Dorothy Nevill finds herself living, in cheerful and garrulous old age, among a new race of Tories who have parted from their convictions—who have in that sense "cut the painter." At present, except Tariff Reform, she says, the Unionists can scarcely be said to have any policy of their own. And why drag in Tariff Reform ? may we ask. It is not the policy of the whole of the Unionist party, by any means. It is lately being dropped at elections. It found no place in the address, and very little in the [speeches, of the successful candidate in Mid- lothian. But that by the way. Lady Dorothy goes on to remark that one of the great delusions of the Unionist Party seems to be the idea that it will gain seats by going one better than the Radicals. In illustra- tion, there comes to hand at the moment the typical instance of Mr F E Smith. That lively gentleman, speaking in an ex cathedra manner that would be more becoming to the leader of his party, told an audience in the North of England what the Tory policy of the future is to be. In the first place, there is to be a great reform of the House of Lords The Unionists, said Mr. SMITH, will make it their business to see that the Second Chamber shall be reconstituted in such a way as to make it command the support of the people_ We should like to hear him saying this in the ear of Lady DOROTHY NEVILL. A House of Lords dependent on the support of the people! A House of Lords that can be altered or reformed in any way without con- stitutional disaster! What would the mid- Victorian Tories have said to such sugges- tions as those which Mr. F. E. Smith makes as lightly and confidently as if they were commonplaces? The candid Lady DOROTHY says that there is now a certain amount of quibbling and hedging about Unionist tactics, and we are glad to have confirmation of our own views from such a source. "The party," she adds, 'seems perfectly incapable of taking a bold line, and saying Thus far will we go and not one inch further' "—of saying to itself, in fact, what Canute said to the sea. The remark is perfectly sound, most indisputably true. There has been hedging and quibbling of the kind. There has been constant repeti- tion of the promise to "go one better than the Radicals." There is an obvious willing- ness to take up any policy whatever that seems likely to catch votes. It is thus that Mr. F. E. Smith's anxiety to reform the House of Lords must be accounted for Reforming the House of Lords is not Toryism. It is " Popkins's plan." But we must credit Mr. Smith with a great object. What he wants is a House—with the people behind it—to fight the House of Commons, also with the people behind it. He would carry on the old contest under new forms, with a new shibboleth; and would have a House of Lords, reformed, talking about being in contact with the people, and yet, as in old days, trampling on popular aspiration.
The awful catastrophe THE DITTON on the railway at DISASTER. Ditton leaves the

public mind particu- larly sensitive to impressions and receptive of suggestions. We hope the same may be said of the official mind. Our visit to the scene of the disaster on Wednesday morning convinced us of the fact that it might have been avoided. The line approaches the station down-hill—a mile of straight with an awful dog-leg curve less than 100 yards from the bridge. The marvel is that so many hundreds of expresses have negotiated the turn with safety. Their drivers must surely , have thanked their patron saints when safely over,and wondered who would be the inevit- able victim. Local residents profess to have anticipated such a smash for years and their statements are credible. Should not the whole question of "taking curves" at express speed be reconsidered by the railway com- panies? There are other danger zones even nearer Warrington about which the. public are distinctly "jumpy," and the opinion is becoming general that too much is. sacrificed to speed. Then there is the question of gas- illumination which, both at Hawes Junction and Ditton, has turned a sufficiently awful smash to a veritable holocaust. It seems to us that the Board of Trade have a cause for intervention here. Electricity would obviate this danger, andlthe Board's own inspectors have more than once advocated its adoption. Such catastrophies as the one at Ditton need to be viewed.in the glaring light that has played round the fate of the Titanic. Sugges- tions are excellent in their way, but let us have something done for the safety of the railway travelling public. The Board of Trade has acted with spirit in regard to the sea-going traveller. It is surely not too much to expect an equal concern and energy on behalf of the railway passenger?

Mr. Borden is not the CRYING "STINKING onl3 Colonial states- FISH." man who has returned to tell his people that the Motherland is neither dead nor dying. In much more vigorous language than Mr. Borden is accustomed to use the Premier of Western Australia said on leaving these shores for home in the summer of 1910 : "1 have motored through your villages on Saturday afternoons and seen sinewy, boisterous boys at play ; I have laughed at the criticisms of England's danger. Don't cry stinking fish, friends, so loudly. You may believe it one day, aud go tumbling to 7gour ruin. lam going back to Western Australia to tell the people frankly that the heart of the Empire is strong." And Sir George Reid,the High Commissioner for the Australian Commonwealth, has said that:

" One of the worst species of the Little Englander' is the man who has a faculty of seeing signs of impotence in the British people, when the current statistics of their trade over- whelmingly prove the very contrary to be the fact." That was in January, 1911. The statistics of to-day show that we are less "impotent " than ever.

Progressive Labour League. Our readers are reminded of the mass meeting to be held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening next, under the auspices of the above League. Mr J J Clancy, M.P., for North Dublin will be the principal speaker and will be supported by Mr Peter Peacock and others. Mr E Wynne Jones will preside.

Successful Athlete. At the Salford Barriers Sports at Belle Vue, Man- chester, on Saturday, H Holbrook, a member of the Warrington Athletic Club, won the first prize in the three-quarrer mile steeplechase by three yards, haviug an allowance of 50 yards. Ile occupied 3cuin. 33 3 ssec. to cover the distance. Peculiar Accident to Veterinary Surgeon's Horse. Mr. Ferguson, veterinary surgeon. was driving from Chester-road, Daresbury, on Monday, when he met a motor waggon. His horse became frightened snd jumped on to some wooden railings at the side of the road, staking itself. Fortunately Mr. Ferguson escaped uninjured. Temperance Rally. In connection with the Band of Hope Conference to be held in Liverpoil next week a temperance rally, promoted by the Warrington Baud of Hope Union, was held in the Co-operative Hall last evening. Mis. James Dodds presided and addresses were given by Miss E. Holmes Harvey and Mr. L. C. M. Cooke. Miss Gornall's Matinee Concert. We have great pleasure in announcing that Miss Mary Gornall has arrang,d an " afternoon concert ' for Thursday, October 17th, to he held in the Con- servative Club. Miss Gornall has been fortunate in securing the services of Miss Evelyn Hall, harpist, a pupil of the great harpist and composer, Herr Pro- fessor Alfred Holy, of the Imperial Opera at Vienna. Miss Hall is a sister of Marie Hall, the celebrated violinist; arid Miss Ameihe Leadbetter, v,oliney cf the Queen's Jail, Patti-Melba Tour. Busoni Tour. Mr William Henry Bleckly, J P., of 1 hetwall T ea, Thelwall, deputy chairman and joint managing director of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Warrington and Wigan, and a director of the Partington Steel Works, now being erected on the banks of the Ship Canal. who died July 2, left £50,763 with net personalty £50,525. Testator bequeathed £5OO to his wife, £lOO to Mr William P Rylands as executor, £5O to his servant Amy Hilda Hayes if still in his service. The residue of his property he leaves to his wife and then for his children. Marriage of Mrs. Henry Waring. Mr. James J. Macpherson, Liberal M.P. for Ross and Croniarty, acted as best man at a wedding on Wednesday last week at St. Clement Dane's Church, Strand, when Mr. Victor Rabagliati, barri-ter-at-law, was married to Mrs. Henry Waring, widow of Mr. Henry Waring, Indian Police and only son of Captain W. Waring of Latchford. The wedding was a very quiet affair. The bride, westing a costume of silver grey satin and a smart hat to match, was' given away by her father, Mr. Bannatyne Macleod. She was attended by three little pages —her son,Master William ' Waring, dressed in white satin, and her two small brothers wearing full Highland costume in the Mackenzie-Macleod tartan. Death of Mr. B. S. Haddock. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death, at the early age of 22 years, of Mr. Bernard Marsh Haddock (eldest son of the late Mr. T. C. Haddock and Mrs. Haddock, of Fearnhead, and nephew of Mr. W. Haddock. engineer of tha Gas Department of the Corporation), who passed away at the Infirmary on Tuesday, following an operation for appendicitis. Mr. Haddock was engaged at the Gas Works at Long- ford as assistant to the engineer, and until Saturday was in sufficiently good health to be able to attend to his duties as usual. Not feeling well he went to spend the week-end with some friends, but became worse, and his removal to the Infirmary was found to be,necessary. He was a keen football enthusiast, who was not content to watch others play, and he took part in his favourite game until a few days before his death. For one so young be bad made a large circle of friends, and his death is deeply regretted. The funeral took place on Friday in the churchyard attached to Christ Church, Padgate. : Male Choirs at New Brighton Eisteddfod. The wisdom of the New Brighton Tower manage- ment, who eleven years ago determined upon an annual musical eisteddfod to be held within the Tower grounds, was further demonstrated on Satur- day when the twelfth celebration of the p ipular fixture took place in the Tower Theatre before large and enthusiastic gatherings. For the thirteen competi- tions on the programme there were no fewer than 181 entrants, the highly-finished performances of some of the competitors eliciting the marked appreciation of the adjudicators, who were Dr W G ill`Naught ;London) and Mr Harry Evans, conductor of the Liverpool Welsh Choral Union. The choral competi- tion for mixed, male and children's choirs were spiritedly undertaken by many well-known contestants from the Principality and the North of England, whose proficiency in their art the audience were not slow to recognise. In the competition for male voice choirs (30 to 40 voices) there were two test pieces : ca) " My love is like a red, red rose" (Bancock), (b) The Beleagured " (Sullivan.; First prize, £2O and a gold medal; second prize, £lO and a silver medal ; third prize, £5 and a silver medal. 1, The St. Helens Glee Xen, 188 points; 2, Todmorden Male Voice Choir, 180 point.; 3, Habergham Glee Union, 181 points. The Warrington Male Choral Union was placed fifth. Mr. Henry Palrclough's Will. Mr. Henry Fairclough, of 27, Wilson Patten-street, Warrington, corn merchant and miller, of Messrs J Fairclough and Warrington. chairman and managing director of the Collins Green Colliery Company, Limited, and a director of Messrs Robinson, Son and Co Ltd, glass manufacturers, of Warriugton,a Member of the Coal Conciliation Board and president of the South-West Lancashire Coalowners' Association, a prominent cricketer formerly assisting in the manage- ment of the County Cricket Club, left A:27,101 gross. He bequeathed £2OO and a further £5O for each five years of service since the date of his will to his servant Anne Low, and 150 and a like additional bequest to his servant Ellen Seddon. He also left £lOO to each of the executors; gun, by Purdy, to his friend, Joel Settle, of Alsager ; china cabinet and its contents and his antique china to his sister-in-law, Alice longton. The residue of the property he left as follows :—One- seventh to his brother, John Fairclough ; one-seventh to his brother, Richard Taylor Fairclough ; one-seventh to his sister, Ellen Dutton ; one-seventh equally between the children of his brother James; one-seventh equally between the children of his sister, Betsy Unsworth ; one-seventh equally between the children of his sister, Mary Ballcarry ; and one-seventh to his niece, Anne Preece, stating that he made no provision in his will for his sister Rachel or her children, as he considered they were well provided for.

CORRUGATED SHEETS and Roofing Felt. Estimates I ree.--J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge at, Warrington.—Advt. Boys Injured in Explosion. A remarkable accident occurred in Oldham-street Latchford, on Sunday afternoon. A detonator, charged with gun-cotton and capable of dislodging a mass of three tons, was exploded by two boys named George Savage, son of John Savage, warehoueeman, and Reginald Goulding, son of Edmund Goulding, both of Oldham-street, with the result that they sustained serious injuries. Goulding, who is ten years of age, lost an eye and his companion had the middle finger of the left hand blown away. It appears that detonators were being used by a workman engaged iaa blasting con- crete beds on ground known as Back'Fields,Latchford. He had fired One charge and before inspecting the result of the blasting operations hid tke remainder of the detonators in a pipe. During his absence a boy of four years found the cartridges, which he carried away to a backyard in Oldham-street and attempted to explode one by striking it with a coal hammer. Evidently the cartridge was not fully charged, for the explosion was only a slight one, and the youngster escaped with a few scratches on the face. He appears to have thrown the detonators into the street, where they were picked up by Savage and Goulding. Savage applied a match to (me of. the cartridges which immediately exploded with terrific force. His left band was severely injured, while his companion's face was much damaged. Savage ran home and 14 detonators were taken from his pocket. He was con- veyed to the Infirmary, where the injured hand was treated. Goulding was taken to the surgery of Dr. Fox who ordered his removal to the infirmary. On Sunday it was found necessary to perform an operation to remove one of his eyes.

div.p: SIGNATURES .1-D. EACH. LOCAL TORIES' COMIC COVENANT. TO BACK U? HAROLD AND ULSTER.

Embellished by the national flag and the motto "Nailed to the mast," a remarkable poster was yesterday affixed to the notice board in the hall of the Conservative Clul3, Sankey-street. The text of the notice reads as follows:
COPY OF TELEGRAM to be sent on Saturday next to Mr. Harold Smith,lM.y., Unionist Headquarters, Old

Town Hall, Belfast. "Please convey to Sir Edward Carson and the Loyalists of Ulster our solemn pledge as citzens of the loyal Borough of Warrington to stand by them in their determination to maintain the unity of Great Britain and Ireland." EVERYBODY WELCOME! SIGNATURES 1/2D. EACH.

Please sign your own name at any of the Unionist Clubs or at the Conser- vative office, Sankey-street. Sir Edward Carson has disclosed the terms of the Ulster Orangemen 's " solemn league and covenant," which few people on this side of St. George's Channel will .believe to be worth the paper it is written on. In fact, it possesses little more value—except his- torically—than the "solemn pledge" from the citizens of the loyal Borough of Warrington.. These plotters of treason are always con- spicuously loyal, before the event. The authors of the precious "league and covenant" refer to themselves as "loyal subjects of his gracious Majesty King George V." and in the next breath pledge themselves to "use all means necessary " to defeat Home Rule, and if carried to refuse to recognise its authority." But it has been left to the Warrington Unionists to crown this solemn farce with the sublimest piece of ridicule. They are going to testify their love for Ulster loyalists by signatures at a ha'penny each. And the Member for the Borough is to present this solemn pledge and its pitiful ha'penny signa- tures to Sir Edward Carson! Could farce, in the guise of serious politics, go further? We hope the electors of this "loyal borough" will take careful note of the messy morass into which their member and the ha'penny party are leading them.

div.head: , WARRINGTON WESLEYAN METHODISM. QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: , WARRINGTON WESLEYAN METHODISM. QUARTERLY MEETING.

• This meeting was held at Padgate on Thursday' Tea was provided by the ladies of the Padgate Church in the new schoolroom, and nearly one hundred repre- sentatives from all parts of the Circuit were present. Thanks to the ladies for their generous hospitalify were heartily accorded on the proposition of Mr. Harris and Mr. Wheatley. Before the company left the tables it was decided to send a message ot con- gratulation, as well as of cheer and hope to Mr. and Mrs. William Bennett, who were away from home ; Mrs. Bennett having recently passed through a serious illness.—Alderman A. Bennett thanked the company in feeling terms for the kindly message. The Rev. W. A. Beckett presided at the business meeting after tea and all the ministers and principal officials of the circuit were present. The Rev. E. Morgan moved a vote of condolence with the relatives of Mrs. Garnett and Mrs. Hartley, both of whom had died since the last meeting. Mr. Morgan spoke of Mrs. Garnett's intense love of Methodism, her deep interest in every part of its work, and her life as a beautiful example of Christian womanhood. Mrs. Hartley had been a generous sup- porter of the church at Latchford and many other good causes. She had done an immense amount of good in so quiet and unostentatious a way dint prob- ably no one would ever know the whole of what she had accomplished. The votes were carried in silence and the Secretary instructed to convey them to the families of the deceased ladies. .

Mr. Harris, Senior Circuit Steward then moved the following resolution :—" This quarterly meeting offers ita hearty congratulations to the Rev J Gunnell on his completion of fifty years in the work of the ministry, it places on record its devout thankfulness for the services he has so willingly rendered to the circuit and prays that the years that remain may be full of peace and happiness." Mr. Harris spoke of the splendid work Mr Gunnell had done in the Warrington circuitl during the past 23 years. The resolution was carried most heartily and Mr Gunnell in replying said that although he could not bear what had been said by the Chairman and Mr. Harris he was sure that all they had said was kindly, appreciative and all too flattering There was one phrase literally true, that spoke of his services " willingly rendered. It was a great joy to him to serve as far as his disabilities allowed. He could only wish that his powers were not being reduced by time and that he could continue still to do as much work as he had done in the past. But while a few years ago be had been able to conduct 100 in the year, now, because his physical powers were failing, be was only able to conduct 32 servicessericee. But what he could do he would do if the friends would only bear with his weaknesses for it was a great joy to him to render service to the fullest extent of his powers. He was gratified to know that the resolution would find a place on the minute book of the proceedings of the quarterly meeting. The Chairman reported the membership to slacw

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S OPERA.
div.p: THE MUSICAL SOCIETY'S OPERA.
"Dorothy."

I The opera section of the Warrington ' Musical Society's members has for some months past, we understand, been busily rehearsing and preparing " Dorothy " for six nights of public performance in the Royal 1 Court Theatre commencing October 7th, and I we would call the attention of our readers to an announcement in another column that the plan of reserved seats will open on Wednesday next. The musical society's choice of another opera on the good old English lines of "Tom Jones" must, we think, be regarded as a wise one, and we have no hesition in predicting for " Dorothy " a popular welcome and a most successful run. With the single exception of the Gilbert-Sullivan collaborations, no comedy opera has achieved so immense a success or so impressed the popular imagination as the picturesque " Dorothy " of a quarter of a century ago—the bright creation of the joint brain of Messrs. B. C. Stephenson and I Alfred Cellier. Nor, until the comparatively quite recent triumphs of Mr. Ed. German's genius, has vocal and dance music of so definitely an old English flavour as that found in Dorothy," been scored in the realm of light opera. Indeed, it is scarcely too much to say that the combination of Cellier's vraceful and singularly appropriate music, with the idyllic story and lyrics provided by Mr. B. C. Stephenson gave us, in Dorothy," a pioneer work which has stamped its easily recognisable impress on many kindred com- positions of the last two decades.
grace]

It will therefore be gathered that in the study and rehearsal of " Dorothy " the Warrington Musical Society has found some- thing worthy upon which members may try their skill, both in music and his- trionics. The older generation of lovers of light opera will recall that the story transports us to the picturesque sur- roundings of the mid-18th century period, and that, in the second of the three acts, the stage picture of "Chanticleer Hall" is, in particular, a dazzling realisation of the triple art of the stage-carpenter, the scenic artist, and the costumier. A gratifying fact too is the announcement that almost all the local people who have made high reputations in the musical society's opera presentations are included in the cast of " Dorothy," while Mr. F. H. Crossley and Mr. R. Walford Lomax are also again at their respective posts of conductor and stage manager. Appended is a list of the dramatis personce:—

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
ARRANGEMENTS FOR NEXT SESSION.

The Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society will open its ninth session on Thursday October 3rd, with every prospect of keen and interesting debates. The object of the society, a most worthy one, is thus briefly set forth in the rules:—" The Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society is established for the purpose of discussing political and social topics accord- ing, as far as may be practicable, to the forms of the House of Commons." Everybody admits that it is desirable for us all to have some idea of the working of the legislative machine, as well as to keep posted up on the great questions of the day, and there is no better means of diffusing this knoa ledge and training young politicians to express their views, than the Par- liamentary Debating Society. A Conservative Ministry will take office and the measures which they intend to introduce will be enumerated in the King's Speech, which will be laid on the table at the business meeting on the 26th mat, when the election of Speaker and other officials of the House will be confirmed. Several prospective Parliamentary candidates have promised to speak at the opening debate on October 3rd. At a special committee meeting on Wednesday evening Mr. James Ball was unanimously reelected speaker of the House; Mr. McDermid, deputy-speaker and chairman of committees ; Clerk of the House, Mr. • E. England; Deputy-Clerk, Mr. B. Pearson; Hon. Treasurer, Mr. J. Ball; Hon. Secretary, Mr. P. A. Jenkins; Assistant Bon. Secretary, Mr. F. R. Isher- wood. The election of Committee WAS deferred until the meeting of the House on the 26th inst. The Conservative Ministry will be led by Ur. E. A. White whose chief supporters will include Mr. W. H. Stansfield, Alderman A. Bennett, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mr. T. Ridgway. The Liberal party will hold a meeting on Tuesday evening to elect the leader of the Opposition and Whips and to make full arrangements for the session's work. It is hoped that the opening of a new session will see a considerable advance in the membership of the society. Anyone wishing to enrol himself can do so by paying 2s. 6d. for the session to the hon. secretary (Mr. F. A. Jenkins), or the party Whirs. Membership cards can be obtained from the political clubs.
