div.head: CROSSING THE LINE.
div.p: CROSSING THE LINE.
LETTER FROM A LOCAL* EMIGRANT.
HOW VOWAWAYS WERE DEALT WITH.

Mr. 11. S. Atkin, recently an auctioneer at Latchford, has sent the following interesting letter written on board the White Star liner, Medic, en route for Australia : August 14th, 1912. Unusual and unique experiences have fallen to the lot of the passengers on board the White Star liner Medic in mid-Atlantic bound for Australia. On the ?boats date we crossed the Equator, the thermometer registering only 75 degrees, tu fact in the early even- ing ladies and gentlemen could be seen wearing coats and overcoats, the wind being quite cool. The heat that we have had so far does not approach the heat that we had in England last summer. I have asked several of the crew who have crossed on several occasions, and they say it is most unusual and that they have never experienced a voyage s, cool and pleasant The second incident was most interesting and exciting. On board the Medic, after we left Liverpool, two stowaways were discovered and on this date also we expected to meet, homeward bound, another White Star liner, the Persic, and rumours were rife on board our ship that the stowaways and passengers' letters were to be put on board the Persic. Excitement ran high during the day and many were the inquiries of the Marconi operator if the Persic was in touch with us. At 6.30 when we went down to dinner a notice appeared that a mail bag would be made up and passed on to the Persic and that letters could be posted up to 9 pm. This news delighted all passengers on board as it meant that we should get letters to our loved ones and friends three weeks earlier than if we bad to wait until we got to Cape Town. After dinner we went on deck again (and as we had been told that we might pass the Persic about 9.30) eyes were watching in front of us for the light of the expected ship. About 9.10 a dim light could be seen in the distance, and the news spread quickly among the passengers that the Persic was sighted. We watched with strained eyes the dim light on the dark waters drawing nearer and nearer until we could see the whole ship beautifully lighted, looking so noble and majestic in the blackness of the night. In the meantime one of the emergency life- boats had been got in readiness and lights fixed. We , watched the lifeboat with its crew, stowaways and letters, being lowered into the sea until it dips the water, and the tiny craft is pitched and tossed like a cork. Many of us quaked with fear as we saw it, thinking it would be swamped. The ropes were lo sed and the brave crew began to pull for the sister ship, and soon the small light disappeared from view, it having reached the Persic. We waited anxiously in the. meantime. Our attention was centered on the Persic and passengers, who could be heard shouting and whistling to us, and we in turn to them, until the hooter of the Persic gave three screams, and we knew then by that signal that the little boat was on its way back to us. We again watch with eager eyes for the light, and when we saw it it seemed to have drifted far away from us. Signals by light are given and answered and the Medic backs to meet the small boat and alternately we could see the small boat now on the crest of a wave, then to disappear again, until it drew to the side of our good ship Medic and in almost less time than I can tell it, it is hauled up and amid shouts and cheers all the crew are safely back on board again. We had by this event had p actical demonstration of what would take place in me event of wreck or disaster. The whole thing passed without a hitch and from start to finish was over in an hour. One of the officers who constituted the crew was the third officer, Mr. 11. Lowe, a survivor of the late Titanic. The event also served to prove to us the enormous value of the' Marconi" system on board ship in being able to locate the exact position of the Persic and to be able to tell almost to the minute the time the two vessels would pass each other. You will have noticed that we were allowed till 9 p m. to post our letters as they expected to pass the Persic about 930 and to the minute we were along side her and at 10.30 had bid farewell to each other. We all retired to our bunks, thankful that we had been permitted to witness what some of the crew who have been at sea for 26 years tell us they had never seen before. We were also thankful for letters dispatched hut sorry for the poor fellows who had caused the excitement as they will, by you receive this, have had to pay the penalty of the law. We also felt that the crew of the Medic would be able to cope successfully and safely with any emergency. 11. S. ATKIN. August 20th, 1912.

div.head: WARRINGTON ATHLETIC CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON ATHLETIC CLUB.
ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING.

There was so enthusiastic gathering of the members I of the local athletic club on Thursday evening, and all appreciated the fact the Pavilion was so near oom- ph4icm ,that it could be used for the annual general meeting. The report of the bon. secretary, Mr C Berry. showed that the club had maintained rs high stand..rd in athletic competitions as the members, from the youngest to the eldest, bad acquired a large share of prizes from the I varir 103 events in which they had taken part as individuals and in cross country running.As a team they had mounted another rung of the ladderms last season's results bad proved the local lads to be the second best team in the United Kingdom, and that Chris Vose had again been selected to represent England in the Inter- national Race and that Herbert Holbrook had added to the athletic reputation of Warrington by rising to the occasion ond gaining a similar honour. Both had been requested to train for the Olympic games and although their abilities and claims to recognition were unques- tionably superior to many selected to travel to Stock- holm, yet their claims were, for some unaccountable reason, overlooked, and indeed it is doubtful if the whole team which represented the United Ringdom in the Cross Country race at the Olympia would have anything to spare if meeting either Hallamshire or Warrington in a team race. The balance sheet and report of the hon. treasurer, Mr R Bennett, showed that there had been a failing off in dotations and that the drawing, dance, and evening sports bad all resulted in a profit the former particularly. The year had opened with a balance in hand of glfi 12s 3d and it spoke volumes for the members and management that after meeting an outlay of £36 2s 9d towards the cost of erecting the pavilion in addition to the usual expenses there was .£2 16a 10d iu hand at the close, and it is hoped that the continued enthusiasm of the members will engender sufficient public patronage to enable the club to continue the good work of pro- viding the accommodation necessary to develop the athletic manhood of the town by encouraging clean healthy sport for its youth. The hard work of the hon, secretary in connection with the erection of the Pavilion and the management of the club generally was recognised by a hearty vote of thanks. The hon. treasurer as also thanked for his splendid services. After such a good year the re-election of otlizials was unanimous except in the case of the committee and two changes were necessary owing to two members being unable, for business reasons, to attend the meetings as required. President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., ; captain, H Holbrook ; vice-captains C Vose and Ei K Jepson ; committee, A Bailie, T lAttersby, C Delman, H Jones, W Price, Tavlin and W Taylor ; auditor, G U Anderton ; hon. treasurer, it Bennett, 194 Gorsey-lane, Warrington ; hon. secretary, C Berry, 9, Bedford-street, Stockton Heath.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING:
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING:

The opening run of Warrington A C. will take place from the Club's Parlour near the Football Ground at 3 n.m. on Saturday next. All members are particularly requested to attend, intending members and visitor 3 are cordially invited. West Lancashire C.C.A. have fixed October sth as the date, and Clock Face Hotel, Clock Face, as the venue for their monstre meet and opening run. Warrington A.C. have arranged several interesting fixtures but the list is not yet complete owing to championship dates not being definitely decided. They have also under consideration a project for federation with four or five other clubs with a view to providing competitions of a suitable kind at athletic sports to be held at various places during the summer of 1913, and all athletes within ten miles of the clubs headquarters should get in communication with the club secretary early so that they can be notified of a special meeting,

EXTRAORDINARY CYCLE FATALITY. Frederick }Bode, aged twenty-one, who resided with his father at Sandiford House, Rushton Tarporley, met his death ander pathetic circumstances, late on Monday night. About 10 p.m. the deceased's brother, Richard Hinde, was walking to Little Budworth, and when near the foot of a very steep hill he heard the sound of a bicycle, and before he could turn round be was struck in the middle of his back and fell on to his knees. When he got up he found that a man and bicycle were lying in front of him. He said to the man " Hey up ; where are you going to ?" but the cyclist, who was lying on his back, did not speak. As the light of the bicycle had gone out Hind(' carried the cyclist on to the grass, and struck a match. and found the cyclist to be his own brother. He obtained assistance from the recreation room mar by, and carried his brother home. Dr Moyes, of Tarporley was summoned, but the injnred man died at 11.15,1 n-clog fractured the base of his skull.

div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE-BOOK.
[By " Silver Street."]
WELLS.

The unlicensed hotel which we had marked in the C.T.O. list was full, but the proprietor said he could recommend a licensed ( ne whose charges were about similar to his own. We had noticed thi4 inn, and put it down as a long way above our pockets. And a thing happened that I never knew before at ODO of these places. When the waiter showed me the room, I took the precaution of asking the price of the room for one night. It was Ss., and I gave him the inevit- able refusal. Ile then consulted the landlord, and we could have it for 4s. fid. As anyone may expect my refusal then was absolute, and although it was raining outside occording to the nature of 1912, we set out to find some place not on our list. We found it at Jefford's unlicensed hotel in Sadler-street, and I may here say I don't know how any one who wishes fora touring holiday on the cycle can have difficulty in finding clean and reasonable places for the night's rest, at least in England, Wales or Scotland. In Ireland I am afraid be would have to rough it a bit, atm I don't know foreign countries at all.

THE CATHEDRAL. I have not seen all the Cathedrals of England, but I should think a visit to Wells is necessary if one would see the finest of all. I used to give the palm to Salis- bury because I consider it is little use building a place of that description without leaving a space all round from which it can be properly seen. That is the drawback of many of our Cathedrals, but Wells is magnificent in every way, both in detail and in total. The Bishop's Palace is a perfect example of work of the Middle Ages, with gateway, drawbridge, and a moat of runniug water. _
Instead of making straight for Bristol we ran along the edge of
THE F.NDIr HILLS.

I have seen that short stretch of road from Wells at Weston described as the finest piece of highway in the country, and it takes a high place in my records. We shall certainly visit it again of all the places in our long tour, and if anyone would see England at its best a railway ticket to Bristol and a week's tour in Somerset with a week for return up the Wye Valley and through Shrewsbury would be almost ideal. Across the wide plain is Wedmore a little village nestling in a hole in the bill side, where AlFerl forced Guthrnm the Dane to sign the treaty restoring the south half of England to its owners ; the Tor at Glastonbury dominates the view for miles, which in the distance lie the Quantocks with Duukerry Beacon bes ond and the hills of South Wales across the Channel. Chedder is wonderful. If it had not been so unfortunate as to be indelibly lined with the word "cheese," its splendid limestone gorge, and wonderland of caves would he more widely known. We left the Mendips with genuine regret and reached Bristol, perhaps the handsomest town in England, late in the afternoon.

div.head: REAR LIGHTS.
div.p: REAR LIGHTS.

I wonder what ;Wed—ilTeni-fUr. Are the search lights on motors proving too expensive? When this period of history comes to be sanely written one thing will stand out pilloried in disgrace with every line of tbe writer, the utter selfishness of the rich bounders who have managed to net so much of the wonderful profits that have come to this land of good fortune. In the factory health and safety must be sacrificed for speeding up of machinery, in the office the clerk has to suffer. On the railway the driver and fireman can go to their doom under the foltplate ; our streets are made into nightmares, and above all our quiet country roads and villages are nowhere safe, just so that the few can hurry the many. And now, when the last of the four sides of a cyclist is lit up, will he be any more safe ? It will simply enable motorists to go so much faster, and indeed such a law intends them to be the chief if not the only beneficiaries. The next law will compel the pedestrian to carry a lamp fixed at the side of his neck (and some need one, I must say.) Curio must have one hung from his tail, Dobbin have a swinging lamp under him ; Tommy must have the soap box on wheel's lighted as he takes his little sister home, and happiest of all, the copper himself will not be allowed to darken his lamp and pounce on us law-breakers suddenly when we are riding on the footpath.

WESLEYAN CYCLING CLUB. Saturday afternoons lately have joined in the general weather topsy-turvy, three out of the last four being cyclists failures, for the fine afternoon has changed to a wet evening. Last Saturday 16 members assembled at the Stag Bridge for a westerly rnn to Mouldsworth, but as the wind was west too, they turned through Hatton to Whitley, Acton Bridge, Crowton and Norley to Ilatchmere. There Mrs Hardman provided an excellent tea, and after waiting some time for the fine weather the glass promised, they discarded the test of the run, and made the same way homewards, hoping that the last two rides, Northenden and Pickmere, may prove more foqunate. Lamp time to-night, 7.12; next Saturday, 6 56.

div.head: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
div.p: ACID STOMACHS ARE DANGEROUS.
NINE-TENTHS OF ALL STOMACH TROUBLE SAID TO BE DUE TO ACIDITY. A PHYSICIAN'S ADVICE ON CAUSE AND
CURE.

A famous physician whose successful researches into the cause arid cure of stomach and intestinal diseases have earned for him an international reputa- tion, said in the course of a recent lecture that nearly all intestinal troubles, as well as many diseases of the vital ergans, were directly traceable to the deranged condition of the stomach, which in turn was ;due nine , times out of ten to excessive acidity, which not only I irritated and inflamed the delicate lining of the stomach, but also set up gastritis and stomach ulcers. It is interesting to note that he condemns the use of patent medicines as well as of medical treatment for the stomach, stating that he and his colleagues have secured remarkable results by the use of ordinary bisurated magnesia, which, by neutralising the acidity of the food, removes the source of the trouble. He contends that it is as foolish to treat the stomach itself as it would be for a man who stepped on a tack to rub liniment on the foot without first removing the tack. Remove the tack and,the foot will heal itself neutralise the acid and stomach troubles will disappear. Irritating medicines and medical treatments are useless, so long as the contents of the stomach remain acid ; remove the acidity and there will be no need for medicine—the inflamed lining of the stomach will then heal itself Sufferers from acidity should get a small bottle of bisurated magnesia from their chemist, and take half a teaspoonful in a quarter of. a glass of hot or cold :water after meals, repeating in fifteen minutes, if necessary, this being the dose which the doctor has found most efficacious in all cases.

Whilst on a street refuge at Hyde Park Corner on Wednesday, Mr Winter, of Oldhill-street, Stoke New- ington, was pinned by a swerving motor 'bus against the pillar of the street refuge, and diedisoon afterwards from his injuries.

div.head: DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A MOTCR CAR.
div.p: DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A MOTCR CAR.

"You are a danger to the public" said the Mayor (Councillor Dr Joseph) to Alfred Boswell, of Wakefield- street,who appeared before the Bench at the Warrington Police Court on Monday on the charge of baying been drunk whilst in charge of a motor car in Legh-street early that morning.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty. P.O Clarke stated that at 1.20 that morning he was on duty in Legh-street when he saw a motor car pro- ceeding from Kendrick-street. As it turned the corner into Legb-street, it almost ran into a shop. Passing along Legh-street it continued to run from one side of the street to the other and witness called to the prisoner, who was driving it, to stop. Prisoner paid no attention to the request. Witness met P.S lienwright in Sankey-street and together they proceeded in the direction of the Lion Hotel garage. in Cairo-street they encountered the prisoner, who WB9 staggering about. They asked him to give an account of his style of driving along Legh-street and he replied "I have not been in Legh-street."Afterwards he admitted that he had been t Liverpool, and that on the return journey he went along Priestley-street, Kendrick-street and Legh-street, and thence to the Lion Hotel. He was beastly drunk. Prisoner said he did not remember what occurred.

P.S. Kenwright stated that prisoner narrowly missed driving the car into an electric standard in Sankey- street, and afterwards he almost ran into Mr H M Ashton's shop. Prisoner said he had had a drink or two, but he was capable of driving. He was not reckless in turning the corner.
The Mayor : You could not be capable of driving, if you were going from one side of the street to the other.
The Chief Constable said it was an offence for a motorist not to stop when called upon by the police to do so.

The Prisoner : I did not hear them. The car is a noisy One. The Chief Constable : I should think that is the truth—that be did not hear them. How on earth he got to the Lion Hotel is a marvel. The Mayor : Did you see them ? The Prisoner : I did not know where they were. (Laughter.) The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been before the Court three times previously, on charges of shop- breaking and drunkenness. It was only on the 13th inst that he received his driver's licence, so that he had made a bad start.

the Mayor (to the prisoner): This is a most serious offence. According to the evidence, you are not fit to drive a motor car. You are a danger to the public. I know something of motor car driving and how careful one has to be. For you, in your drunken condition, to be driving a car, was a terrible thing. The Bench will be lenient with you as far as the fine is concerned, but they are only sorry they cannot take your licence from you. You are not lit to be let loose. You will be fined 108. and costs and your licence will be endorsed.

div.head: Borough Police Court. TUESDAY.—Before C )uncillors H Roberts (in the
div.p: Borough Police Court. TUESDAY.—Before C )uncillors H Roberts (in the

chair) and C Jackson Holmes, Messrs J Rymer Young and T Locker. A BICYCLE THlEF.—Robert Cunningham, of no fixed address, was charged with stealing a bicycle, value £3, the property of William Foster, of Dutton-street. The Chief Constxble stated that on September sth, the prisoner met a little boy named Thomas Giblan aud inquired where he could hire a hicycle. The boy told him he could get one at Mr Fosters shop and accompanied him there. Prisoner gave his name as Cunningham and said he wanted to hire a machine for a couple of hours. Prosecutor lent him a machine and he dis- appeared, nothing more being heard of him until Sunday night when a telephone messag4 was received from Doncaster to the effect that prisoner bad surrendered there and had admitted having stolen a bicycle at Warrington. Prisoner now stated that the machine was taken from him as soon as he arrived in Manchester.—ln order that the police might make inquiries as to the disposal of the machine and the antecedents of the prisoner, the magistrates ordered a remand for a week.

Tit I.7nSDAY—Before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair) and Messrs NV Roberts, A J Jolley, %V T Williams J Upson and Dr Nader,. W IFH ASSAULT.—WiIIiam James Blaze, 117, Bostock- street, was summoned for assaulting his wife Louisa Blaze,on September 12th.—MrIF It Rober.ta,who appeared for the complainant,stated that on the night in question defendant was drinking with some friends at the back of the shop. After the friends had gone home defendant came into the shop and abused his wife about his , supper. The wife retorted that she was not going to ' base the men drinking at her home. Defendant con- cealed himself behind the curtain and when complainant came out of the shop he struck her a violent blow in the mouth with his fist.—Defendant denied that he struck his wife. She had goaded him on to strike her many times but he had refrained from doing so.—The magistrates decided he had committed a common assault and a fine of 12s or 7 days was imposed.

div.head: WORLD'S TEA CADDY.
div.p: THE WORLD'S TEA CADDY.

Under this title the " Tea and Coffee Trade Journal " of New York describe the Kidderpore Tea Warehouse at Calcutta and the operations conducted there. In Iconcluding the article, the writer says :—" We bear a good deal about Java tea in these days and its improv- ing quality, but those who tell us about it seem never anxious to inform the world that the improvement in Java tea is really due to the fact that Java has been in recent years, and is now being, planted throughout with tea seed taken from the gardens throughout India. Surely no greater compliment to the excellence of a country's products can be paid than this. India fears no rival, for nowhere in the world is finer tea produced than throughout the various dietricts of India. It is due to this fact that the largest Russian buyers have come to Calcutta and opened establishments of their own, knowing full well that the demand for Indian tea, which has in the past few years become so great in Russia, is with them to stay. It is due also to the fact that Indian tea is so rapidly increasing in demand in all markets that during the year just ended the quotation for ordinary clean leaf Indian tea attained in October a figure approximately twice what similar tea could be bought at only four years ago, and this in spire of the season of 1911-1912 being the most prolific in yield ever known in the his- tory of 'lndian tea productions. In India to-day well over half a million acres is planted with tea, which will convey an idea of the magnitude of this industry and the amount of money that has been invested in the pro- duction of the leaf so popular the world over. The writer advises travellers who may he visiting Calcutta and who are interested in this wonderful in- dustry, not to miss seeing what, be thinks, may be aptly termed "The World's Tea Caddy," Mr. Gothen the superintendent, will be always pleased to welcome them and make the visit an enjoyable cne.

div.head: Christ Church, Latchford.
div.p: Christ Church, Latchford.

The harvest thanksgiving services were held on Thursday. There was a celebration of Holy Com- munion at 7.45, morning prayer at 10 and evening prayer at 8 o'clock. The last service was fully choral, Mr T L Fry, the organist and choirmaster, presiding at the organ. The Magnificat was T H Maunder •s setting in C, and the anthem " The eyes of all uait upon Thee," by Dr Charles Vincent. The whole service was, as usual, beautifully rendered. The preacher was the Rev IV S Adams, assistant curate of airesbury, and formerly chaplain to the leper asylum at Emjanyana, Cape Colony, who preached an eloquent sermon from the text,Ecclesiastes, xii , 13., " Fear God." The church had been beauti- fully decorated, the font, choir screen, and sanctuary being particularly attractive. The collections through- out the day were given to the Assistant Curacy Fund. The services will be continued on Sunday.

St. Barnabas' Church. This church had been very tastefully decorated for thi. harvest thanksgiving services which commenced on Thursday. There was a plentiful supply of flowers, fruit, cereals and vegetables, and they had been arranged with pleasing effect by the lady workers. The altar, font and pulpit received special and artistic treatment. There was a good congregation at evensong which was conducted by the Vicar (Rev. J. H. G. Hol lingworth). The preacher was the Rev. H. W. Trott, vicar of Saighton, near Chester, who referred to the fadi that many people had recently been questioning thi wisdom of holding harvest thanksgiving services, in view of the prolonged spell of wet weather and con- sequent partial failure of the crops. lie pointed out that we were not dependent on our own resources for our food supplies, which were world-wide in their origin, and we ought, therefore, to be thankful that we were at peace with other nations. Harve at thanks- giving services were held to express gratitude not only for food but for all temporal blessings. The choir sang the anthem " I will feed My flock " (Simper), Mr T Evans presiding at the organ. The collection was OD behalf of the choir fund.

Christian Re-union. Bishop of Liverpool and Cautious Advances. Speaking at an inaugural meeting on NVednesday evening at the Liverpool University in connection with a series of twelve Extension Lectures which are to be held under the auspices of the Liverpool Diocesan Sunday School Institute and the Liverpool Sunday School Union, The Bishop of Liverpool said the days of the old-fashioned Sunday school were numbered, but never was there greater opportunity for Sunday school work which was up-to-date than at the present. At a time when be believed that the heart of the English people was more religious than ever, but when one of their great needs was definite and clear teaching of the NVord of Cod, nothing could be more important than that those who were teaching the rising generation should know clearly what they had to teach and how they ought to teach. "1 am one of those,' declared his lordship, "who desires passionately the re-union of Christendom. lam most strongly of opinion that that re-union in England should begin with the Churches of the Reformation. While, on the one hand, I deprecate most strongly, as many of you do, any. premature and rash and impulsive steps towards re-union which in the long run will be likely to binder the object we have at heart, I do welcome and thank God for every movement that seems to prepare for that great day when we shall be all one flock and one shepherd." There were two such movements at present which were doing much to prepare the way. There was the great student volunteer movement. None of them csuld forget the inspiration they received at the meet- ings held some months ago in the Philharmonic Hall, when Churchmsn and Nonconformists stood side by side on the platform, one in their desire to spread the kingdom of our Lord, and yet neither one nor the other compromising one little bit their own principles and convictions. The second great snovement which would prepare the way to reunion was the reform of the Sun- day school. It is bringing together the teachers, the very life-blood of their congregations, both Church and Nonconformist. It was a wonderful thought that week after week that theatre should be crowded by Church people and Nonconformists listening to any Church t,acher and any Nonconformist teacher, :forgetting for a time their differences, losing their prejudices, and realising how very much they had in common. (Applause.) Buckley-street P.S A. Society, The half-annual distribution ot prizes took place on Sunday last at three o'clock. Mr. Smethurst occupied the eclair, and Mrs. Smethurst kindly distributed the prizes. Mr. Turton delighted the audience with his rich baritcme voice, and Miss Hockenhull sweetly rendered " The Better Land," whilst Mr. Syers was much appreciated for bis violin solo. There was a good gathering, and all had a very pleasant afternoon. Miss Lea was the pianist.

St. John's Presbyterian Church. On Sunday evening, dealing with the prophet poten- tial end the prophet actual, Mr. Reid stated that the power to penetrate the thin veil existing between the visible and the invisible was necessary to, but did not constitute, the prophet. To be able to get other people to see what he saw, to interpret his own vision to others in terms they could understand were the marks Of the true prophet, and life in all its aspects opened out as a wide field of action in this connection. Because Christ, the greatest Interpreter of all, was able to interpret the Father, manifesting prophethood at its highest, He had made it to an extent obligatory to all. Some, because of their responsiveness, were led by the open vision, while others, because of incapacity, were led by the pathway of a dark discipline ere the eyes could be opened to see the wondrous things in God's law. Warrington Sunday School Union. An inspiring scene was presented in Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday afternoon .vhen the War- rington and District Sunday School Union held its first united service. The attendance, which was fully representative of the Nonconformist denominations, numbered nearly 1,600, the chair beiag occupied by the Rev. William Reid, president of the Union, who was supported by the Baptist ministers. After the opening hymn " Onward, Christian soldiers," prayer was offered by the Rev J S Chedburn and Scripture read by the Rev W A Beckett. Miss Ella Cottam gave the recita- tion "The last hymn " with much feeling. In the course of his address, the President said they believed that to-day with the ever-increasing strain brought by succeeding years, the spirit which worked through federation to successes in nearly every depart- ment of life would in this uniting of Sunday school interests and forces be found to achieve results far more valuable and successful than any that have or could be realised under the less desirable conditions of isolation. He wanted all the scholars and teachers to hive a widened vision of their life and work; and every school also. It was quite true that each school had its own problems of which only it could work out the solutions, and the same was true of each teacher and scholar ; but, while each must bear his own burden there was such a thing as bearing each other's burdens, in its way as indispensable as the other, and only possi- ble when united. The Union leaders were anxious for this, and, In addition to conferences and visita- tions, would remind the teachers of the Teachers' Training Centre which had been initiated, and the scholars and teachers of Scripture examinations, arrangements for which were now being pushed forward and when completed would be communicated to the secretary of each school.

After the collection, which realized over .C 4 the con- gregation joined in singing the bymm, "Stand up, stand up, for Jesus," Mr. T. 11. Ackroyd, whose work among the destitute children of Manchester renders him n most acceptable speaker, next addressed the meeting his remarks creat- ing a great impression on the boys and girls. The sing- ing of another hymn terminated the service.

Wycliffe P.S A. Society. There was an exceptionally good meeting on Sunday last, presided over by Mr. B Farrar, president, when a visit was paid by the Rev. J. G. Gascoigne, president of the Lancashire and neighbouring Counties Federa- tion of P.S.A'S. and kindred societies,who spoke words of inspiration sod encouragement to the brethren, to whom he was glad to pay presidential visit. He referred to the National Federation Conference now being held in Manchester. The Fres Trade Hall meet- ing last Saturday night was an inspiring one. The meeting was addressed by Bishop Went:ton of Man- chester, Rev. Silvester Horne M.P., William Ward. and Harry Jeffe,the latter now being the National Federation President. There were representatives from France, Belgium. Canada, and other places representing the three-quarter million brotherhood, men in this and other lands. The Conference lasted until Wednesday. He urged the Wycliffe P.S.A. brethren to an effort to bring in the men outside. Mr. McEachren took part in the meeting and five new members received a hearty welcome. A vote of sympathy was passed to the President on the death of hie brother, also to 3/r. Healey on the death of his sister.

Wycliffe Congregational Church. The pulpit at this church on Sunday was occupied by the Hey. J. G. Gascoigue, of Stockport-road Congrega- tional Church, Msnchester. His address to the children was based upon the verse :

The life that counts must toil and fight, Must hate the wrong and love the right ; Must live for truth by day by night This is the life that counts. De pointed out that it was not money or fine clothes that counted, bat character. It was not what they had but what they were. In his sermon he spoke on the necessity for faith, taking for his text the words" According to your faith be it unto you." (Matthew ix., 29.) The circum- stances of our times, he said, demanded faith in God. It was certainly true that they could not receive any ocular demonstration of God, and they must therefore proceed with the light of faith to discover God. They must believe that He was the rewarder of them who diligently sought Him. It was not enough to get back to protoplasm and arrive at the conclusion that life might be the result of a chemical combination. We wanted something more than that. We wanted to see at the back of protoplasm and at the back of all things, a Creator, an iatelligent mind, a loving heart which still ruled and which was still on the Throne. We murt settle it in our hearts, first that God is, and that He was able and willing to bless, faithful to defend, wise to rule and worthy to be obeyed. As aids to faith the preacher pointed out that God was discoverable to the pure in heart, was respon- sive in communion, and was to be found along the road of service. He proceeded to show that faith had made heroes and heroines, and asked his hearers to have faith in themselver and work so as to bring God's Holy City to Warrington. In the evening Mr Gascoigne's sermon was based on John xix., 5.," and Pilate said' Behold the man. " In introducing his subject the preacher salted his hearers to have in mind also another passage" Is not this the Carpenter ? " Human origin and destiny were very great. Man had been created a little lower than the angels. He was crowned with glory and honour. It was true the crown was often in the dust, but our God was Redeemer as well as Creator and had always sought through the ages those who were responsive to His spirit. Hence the long list of saintly heroic men and women, culminating in Jesus as the pro-eminent man enthroned above all. " Behold the Man" supremely in touch with human life, no ascetic or stoic, but having full control ot His human nature he revealed the inherent greatness of man ennobled and exalted by communion with God.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Two of Mr. Pied Karno's Companies practically supply the programme at the Palace and Hippodrome this week. A couple of characteristically humorous sketches are presented, the first being " Mr. Justice Perkins," which has won a warm welcome on previous visits. Albert Bruno is screamingly funny as Perkins, J.P., and the court scene, with its travesty of justice, evokes roars of laughter. If we are not mistaken, " Perkins in Paris," is new to Warrington theatre-goers. It is one of the best extrava- ganzas in two scenes that Karno has yet pro- duced, and occupies something like 40 minutes to present. The first scene depicts an art-school in Paris, where we see a crowi of youthful pupils clamouring for live " models," and a pompous pro- fessor who reluctimtly consents to the innovation. .Our friend Bruno, as Perkins the studio caretaker, provides the models and submits them for inspection with an amount of drollery which is incredibly mirth-provok- ing. The " action" then passes on to the ballroom at the . Countess of Lemonton's, where Perkins again distinguishes himself by appearing in uniform and fighting a very comic duel with a French officer. Both scenes are elaborately mounted, and the company is both numerous and capable. Miss Julia Bassett and Miss Elsie Love both play prominent parts with grace and skill. In addition to the Karno productions there are other attractive items in the bill. The Five Jovers present a very expert gymnastic and acrobatic act, full of thrills and feats which are an novel and daring. Alf Gibson is the original comical exponent of the quiet style of humorous singing, and Dorothy Leigh obliges with songs which are above the average in quality and reveal her undoubted talent as a comedienne. A smart song and dance duo is supplied by the Sisters Simms, and the Donatos, the famous-one-legged clowns, also entertain in a way which would be difficult to imitate. The orchestra is very efficient, but this week, at any rate, inclined t) be noisy.

div.head: Closing Years.
div.p: Closing Years.
REPRESSION BY ROYAL DECLARATION.

_ In high places, as in low, the smart betrayed itself. The Bishops combined to exert pressure upon the King,and in February 1675, wearied in his efforts for Toleration, he issued the Royal Declaration, which left Nonconformists entirely at the mercy of their persecutors. By this document Charles declared "that he found it necessary that the law should be put in operation with more care than of late had been, and had resolved and did order that effectual care be taken for the Suppression of Conventicles." His Majesty proceeded to declare that all licences were long since recalled and that no licence had any authority or encouragement from him. The hands were the hands of the King,but the voice was the Bishop's voice.

Upon some the blow fell heavily. Nathaniel Heywood put his feelings in pathetic sentences, and they are to be quoted here because they give the only glimpse that the period affords us of Robert Yates. Whether the withdrawal of the Indulgence increased his persecutions we have no means of knowing, but he appears in the quotation as a man almost broken under the strain of heavy years. "Oh, this goes heavily" cries Heywood "I think this turning out of our licenced places will cost Mr. Yates and myself our lives. Our casting out of our great places was not so much as casting us out of our little places. Other afflictions are light compared with a dumb mouth and a silent Sabbath."

div.head: NONCONFORMITY TAKES SHAPE.
div.p: NONCONFORMITY TAKES SHAPE.

Nonconformity must now take its own chances in the world. The King's declaration that its meetings should be suppressed removed the last shadow of Royal protection. Its power to live and flourish must hence- forth conic from within. It must take its own place and achieve its own destiny. The brief months of liberty had closed abruptly with the King's ban. But no Royal order could stay the movement that had been started, and it was clear that no law making could enforce conformity. Puritanism came through its fiery ordeal. Slowly and against many trials the Noncon- formist bodies organised themselves. Ordina- tion services, unknown among Presbyterians since the Reformation, were re-established and Presbyterian ministry became an ordered reality. Independents, Baptists and Quakers shaped themselves after their own ideal and prepared to take their part in the long and toilsome warfare that was to win in one age toleration and in the next religious liberty. But only their children's children far removed were to see the fruits of their sufferings.

div.head: _ROBERT YATES.
div.p: _ROBERT YATES.

Of Robert Yates, SO courageous in all we learn of him, we would fain know more; but he had no biographer and it is now too late to supply the omission. The Parish Registers contain his frequent autograph and notes, all written in a scholarly hand. Some events of his life there recorded may for convenience be grouped together here. The burial of his first wife is recorded in 1652. November. Buried Elizabeth wife to Mr. Robert Yeats Parson the 6th day. Two years later he is married in the Parish Church to Mrs. Martha Hordley. 1654 October. Married Mr. Robert Yeats to Mris. Martha Hordley the 3 day. Yet another two years and an event of deep jimportance cheers him. This is the birth of his son Samuel whose setting apart for the ministry has already been referred to. The advent is recorded with what, in a Church Register, may be regarded as quite a wealth of detail. 1656 November. Christened Samuel son to Mr. Robert Yeats Rector the 18 day and was borne the 14 day of the same month at six of the clocke in the morninge. HIS WILL

His will was prepared in 1674. It is written in his own hand upon a single sheet' of small foolscap the bottom portion of which has suffered from damp and decay whilst lying in the Chester Probate Registry. We quote as much as can be deciphered. Let it be remembered that the eight and twentieth day of December in the yeare of our Lord 1674 and in the six and twentieth yeare of the raigne of our sovereign lord King Charles the second over England etc. Robert Yates of Warrington in the Ccunty of Lancaster, clerk, being in bodily health and of perfect remem- brance do for the quiet of my mind and the settling of my temporal estate make this present writing containeing therein my last will in manner and forme following, that is to say that

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 21, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 21, 1912.

whereas I stand possessor of a tenement be'ng the one half of Banck Hall together with the out- howseing and land thereunto belonging lying and situate in Broughton in the County of Lancaster bought and purchased by me of Richard Taylor of Prestwich. Concerning which tenement my mind and will is that the yearly rent and profits thereof shall be equally divided every year betwixt my deare wife Martha Yates and my naturall son Samuel Yates during the naturall lives of both of them and my mind and will is that after the death of one of them the whole profitts shall go to the other that shall survive during his or her naturall life. And after the death of them both our said son Samuel leaving neither wife nor child alive my mind and will is that the whole tenement and tenant right of it diall go t-i my naturall brother John Yates and, if he be dead, to his children, to be equally divided among for as many as shall be living provided that he or they shall pay my son Samuels debts and funerall expenses out of the first profits of the said tenement. And as for my personall estate or the remainder thereof my mind and will is that my son Samuel Yates shall have all my books except- ing for as many as any wife Mai tha Yates shall desire to have for her own use and as concerning the rest of my personal estate whether gocds or effects I give and bequeath them all after my debts and funeral expenses are paid to my dear wife leaving it to her discretion to give out parts thereof as she pleaseth to my said son Samuel and when and how she pleaseth and this I do not for want of love and natural affection to my son. . . • My dear brother William Yates of Blackburn I do appoint overseer of this my will. I revoke and make void all former wills. . • I appoint my deare wife Martha executrix. . . . CLOSING DAYS. _ _

Calamy prepared a brief sketch of Robert Yates in his "Sufferings of the Nonconfor- mists" and we depend upon the few lines there written for our knowledge of his latest years: " When ha was afterwards ejected for his Noncon- formity, he bad scvetal potent enemies, who brought him into some trouble by the Five Mile act. In 1672, be took the opportunity of preach- ing in a public meeting-house, but was violently disturlycd. He was rim t long afterwards si( zed by a palsy which affected his intelhetuals, and rendered him incapable of his work a year before he died ; which was in November 1073 aged 60." . .

The "Northowrarn Register," a list of dates and records made by his friend Oliver Heywood, has the brief entry Mr. Vales of Wairington N. C. rninr struck with a ralsie, lcst his intellectualls, lay long,

died Nov-. 1678 ; his wife died ffebruary after. Both of these records are incorrect in the matter of date. The Warrington Register shows his burial in the churchyard in October 1678. 1678. October. Euritd. Mr. Robeit Yaatts Mkister the 28 day. An entry four months later records the burial of his widow. Bun if d ffehruary 1678. Allis Ma tha Yaathis of Church Street Widow the 25th day. The life that had reached its lingering close left its mark upon Warrington. Robert Yates was a typical Nonconformist of the unyielding type. Persecution might break his health, but it could not daunt his spirit. Such fortitude is contagious, and it lived on in his congregation long after the wearied brain and body had broken under the strain. The church like its founder was typical. It belongs to the general movement, and whatever of value attaches to that move- ment, or whatever of honour is due to its pioneers, belongs to the early Nonconformists of Warrington. To be Continued. A.M.

div.head: ORIGIN OF HOME RULE.
div.p: THE ORIGIN OF HOME RULE.
By the Late A. M. Sullivan, K.C„ M.P.

Mr. A. M. Sullivan, one of the most brilliant orators of the last generation and a well-known leader in the Temperance Movement, published his personal reminiscences in a charming volume, "New 11 eland," from which the following sketch of the foundation of the Home Rule movement is taken. _

On the evening of Thursday, the 19th of May, 1870, a strange assemblage was gathered in the great room of the Bilton Hotel, Dublin. It was a private meeting of some of the leading merchants and professional men of - the metropolis, of various political and religious opinions, to exchange views upin the condi- tion of Ireland. Glancing round the room, one might ask if the millennium had arrived. Here were men cf the most opposite parties, men who never before met in politics save as irreconcilable fees. The Orange- man and the Ultramontane, the staunch Conservative and the sturdy Liberal, the Nationalist Re; ealer and the Imperial Unionist, the Fenian sympathiser and the devoted loyalist, sat in free and friendly counsel, discussing a question which any time for fifty years prevLusly would have instantly sundered such men into a dozen factions arrayed in stormy conflict. "What, can we do for Ireland 7" they asked. The Protestant, Conservatives spoke up. Some of them were men of large property as country gentlemen ; others were amongst the wealthiest and most influen- tial merchants of the metropolis. " It is impossible for us," they said, " to view the events of the past five years without feeling it incumbent on us as we value the welfare of our country and regard the safety and security of all we possess, to make some step towards a reconciliation or agreement with the national sentiment. In that sentiment, as we under- stand it, there is much we cannot assent to. Some of the designs associated with it shall ever encounter our resistance. But we have never concealed from ourselves, and indeed have never denied, that in the main the aspiration for national autonomy is one which has sound reason and justice, as well as his- torical right behind it. We wish to be frank and clear we will hive no part in disloyal plans; we will have no separati in from England. But we feel that the scheme of one pailiament for all purposes,itnperial and local, has been a failure ; that the attempt to force consolidation on the Irish people, to destroy their national individuality, has been simply disastrous. However attractive in theory fir imperial statesmen, that project has utterly broken down in fact and reality. It has c at us perpetual insecurity, recurrent insurrection. It may suit English politicians to cling to the expeiimrnt still, and pursue it through

himself, so to speak, in the prolonged and desperate effort of their defence. No wonder that in 1868 he had earned their gratitude and won their confidence. Four years of such sad work meanwhile wrought powerfully with his sympathic nature. In 1869 he accepted the position of President of the Amnesty Asscciation, and soon became the one great figure in Irish popular politics. Immediately on the fall of the Irish Church be saw what was coming in Ireland. He knew the feelings— the fears the hdpes, the questionings—that surged in the breasts of his fellow-Protestants. He determined to use the gi eat power which now rested with him in an endeavour to close for ever the era of revolt and bloodshed, to unite in a common work of patriotism Irishmen long divided by class and creed distinctions; and to establish between Ireland and England a union c f friendship and justice which might defy the shocks of time.

At this Bilton Hotel conference be listened long to the utterances of his fellow-Protestants, many of them the familiar associates of his college days. He marked , their fears about disloyalty, their apprehensions that the Fenians and the Romanists would be content with nothing less than separation. He rose to his feet and spoke with great earnestness. 'lt is we, it is our inaction, our desertion of the people and the country, the abdication of our position and duties, that hare cast these men into the eddies and whirlpools of rebellion," he said. "If you are but ready to lead them by cot stitutional courses to their legitimate national rights, they are ready to follow you. Trust me, we have all grevionaly wronged the Irish Catholics priests and laymen. As for the men whom mis- government has driven into revolt, I say for them that if they cannot aid you they will not thwart your experiment. Arise! Be bold ! Have faith, have con- fidence, and you will save Ireland ; not Ireland alone, but England also !" He concluded by proposing : That it is the opinion of this meeting that the true remedy for the evils of Ireland is the establishment of an lush parliament with full control over our domestic affairs.

The Chairman put the resolution to the meeting. "As many as ate of opinion that this resolution do pass say Aye ' " A shout of ' Aye ' rang through the room. "The contrary will say `No.' Not a dis- sentient voice was heard. Then every one, greatly astonished, burst into a checT—the first beard that evening, so grave and earnest and almost solemn had been the tone of the deliberations. This was the birth of the Irish Home Rule move- ment.

It will be understood, of course, that this was merely the beginning of the Home Rule movement, as we know it to-day. There had been a continuous a esistance of the Act of Union fram the day it passed into law in IBoo,but prior to the events related herein, the Irish nati nal demand was for a repeal to the union.

div.head: IiCHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: IiCHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
A BOY'S ESSAY ON POLITENESS.

Politeness is rather a difficult thing, especially when you are making a start. Many people haven't got it. I don't know why, unless it is the start. It is not polite to fight little boys, except they throw stones at you. Then you can run after them and, when you've caught them, just do a little bit at them, that's all. Re- member that all little boys are simpletons or they wouldn't do it. It is not the thing to make fun of a little chap because he is poorer than you. Let him alone if you don't want to play with him, for he is as good as you except the clothes. When you are in school, and a boy throws a bit of bread or anything to you over the desks, it is not polite to put your tongue out at him, or to twiddle your fingers in front of your nose. Just wait till after school, and then warn him what you'll do next time ; or, if you find you are bound to hit him, be pretty easy with him. Don't keep on eating after you are tightening, and you will be far happier. Never eat quickly, or you might get bones in your throat. My father knows of a boy who got killed over his Sunday dinner. It is not polite to leave victuals on your plate, especially anything you don't like. If you don't like turnips, it is better to eat well into your turnips first while you are hungry, and you'll eat the meat and potatoes easy enough afterwards. Boys should always be polite to girls, how- ever vexing they may be. Girls are not so strong as boys, their hair is long, and their faces are prettier ; so you should be gentle with them. If a girl scratches you on the cheek, don't punch her, and don't tell her mother. That would be mean. Just hold her tight by the arms till she feels you could give it to her if you had a mind to.

AT GRANDMA'S. When the gatepcst hardly lifts Its square head above the drifts When the coast is smooth and white, And the windows frost at night, I like to be at grandma's. When the yellow chickens peep And the grass begins to creep, When we hear the bluebird's trill And the frog king's piping shrill I like to be at grandma's.

When the currants burn and glow, And the blackberries dusky grow, When there's fun the whole long day When the men are making bay, I like to be at grandma's, When the maple leaves turn red And the popcorn's harvested, Apples in the cellar bin, Pears and nuts all gathered in, I like to be at grandma's. Well, I guess that that's 'bout all, Spring and summer, winter, fall, I have made it seem quite clear That 'tie right around the year I like to be at grandma's. —ANNIE M. L. HAWES. SOME BOYS' ANSWERS.

Boys are always writing or saying funny things (at least so the teachers say), and an American schoolmaster has been lately telling us that he got the following answers in a Scripture examinatian. " Manna is being polite." "Jerusalem was surrounded with walls to keep in the milk and honey." "Jacob was a patriarch by trade. In them days people lived on corn, like horses do now. They always called it pudden and porridge messes. Jacob could eat a good mess, but Esau, who was the oldest, could not eat as much as you might think. The patriarch Moses never eat nothing except when there was a famine."

div.head: KING'S HEADQUARTERS AT CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: THE KING'S HEADQUARTERS AT CAMBRIDGE.

During the Army Manceuvres this week, can be seen stretching from the bay windows the King made Trinity College, Cambridge, to the extreme left. Our picture also shows his headquarters. The Royal apartments are the entrance under military guard. in the Master's Lodge. The windows of them

another fifty years, always "just going to succeed this time ;" but for us Irish Protestants whose lot is east in this country, and whose all in the world is within these seas, it is time to think whether we cannot take into our own hands the solution of this problem. We want peace, we want security, we want loyalty to the Throne • we want connection with England ; but we will no fonger have our domestic affairs committed to a London Parliament. The question is whether we can agree upon an arrangement that would harmonise those national aspirations in which we largely partici- pate, with that imperial connection which we desire to retain." Such was the tenor and substance of a discussion or conversation which extended upwards of an hour. The probability of certain taunts being levelled at them Was discoursed upon. "It will be said we are uttering these sentences now out of spite against England for disestablishing our Church " (which was quite true of some of them.) "As to that, we freely say two considerations have hitherto ruled us : Firstly, to the covenant with England in re'erence to our Church we certainly were faithful. Some of us regretted that bargain, and boldly avow, now that England has violated it, that we feel more free as Irishmen, and shall be none the worse as Protestants. Secondly, we did entertain, no doubt, an apprehension as to bow Roman Catholics, who are numerically the balk tif this nation, might exercise their political power under the pressure of ecclesiastical authority. As to the first consideration, the Act of Union is now dissolved ; the covenant has been torn up. As to the second, reading the signs of the times, we believe we may . fearlessly dismiss the suspicions and appre- hensions that have hitherto caused us to mistrust our Roman Catholic countrymen." Sitting silently observant of this remarkable scene was a man who perhaps more than any other living Irishman held in his hands the political destinies of• the country at that moment. Isaac Butt was born at Glenfin, Co. Donegal, in 1815, being the son of the Protestant rector of that place. He was educated at Trinity College, Dublin, where he rapidly rose to dis- tinction. He had barely passed his majority when he was elected to the professorship of political economy in the University of Dublin. Ile was called to the Bar, in November 1838, and made a Queen's Counsel in 1844, one of the few Irish advocates who wore "silk" at the age of 29. From his earliest college ' days he was a politician, and 30 years ago he was the rising hope of the Irish Protestant Conservative Party. Ile was their youthful champion selected in 1841 to do battle against O'Connell himself in a great four day debate on Repeal in the Dublin Corporation. All Tory as young Butt was, he had a thoroughly Irish heart, and an intense love of the principles of liberty. i In the debate with O'Connell, it s remarkable to note that he confined himself almost entirely to an argu- ment that the Union experiment had not been fully tried. At the close of the encounter his great antagonist, after paying a high tribute. to his genius,l prophesied that Isaac Butt would one day be found "in the ranks of the Irish people." Early in 1852 he was invited by the English Conservatives to stand for Harwich, which borough he represented up to the dissolution in the summer of that year, when he was, as we have noted elsewhere, returned for Youghal. At the bar he attained a high position. Retook a leading part in all the great trials, civil and political, from 1844 to the State prosecutions just concluded. He for a time gave himself up almost exclusively to a parliamentary career. In 1864, how- ever,he was called from London to Ireland, to conduct one of the most important mercantile causes of the period. At its close, instead of returning to Parlia- mentary pursuits, he ceased to attend the House of Commons, and devoted himself more closely than ever to professional labours. In 1865 he stood facile princeps in the front rank of Irish advocates. The Fenian prisoners, beset by many and serious difficulties as to their defence, turned to him as one whose name alone was a tower of strength. Not in vain did they appeal to his chivalrous generosity, his love of con- stitutional liberty, his sympathy with those struggling against the severities of power. He flung himself with ardour to their side ; and once his feelings were aroused and hia sympathies enlisted in their fate, he never gave them up. For the greater part of four years, sacrificing to a considerable extent a splendid practice in more lucrative engagements, he buried

div.head: SEVEN YEARS' RECORD.
div.p: SEVEN YEARS' RECORD.
Greatest Measure of the lika.

Dr. T. J. Macnamara, M.P. (Financial Secretary to the Admiralty) addressed a meeting of Young Liberals at the Coburg-road Schools, North Camberwell, on Saturday evening. He said the record of Radicalism for the past seven years justifibel the keenest enthusiasm and their most untiring energy. They had entered upon great commitments on behalf of the working people,but they had so shifted the incidence of taxation as in no wise to cause the burden of taxation falling upon the working classes to be increased. On the contrary, they had reduced taxation, in particular as it affected them. (Hear, hear.) They had reduced the tea tax and the sugar tax, and they had wiped out £61,000,000 of national debt. Yet notwithstanding that fact, they were now finding in this year over £12,000,000 for old age pensions (Applause.) There were at this moment very nearly a million old folk sitting at home enjoying those old age p3osions. (Hear, hear.) Further still, in the field of social reform, they had brought into being the greatest instrument for sectring the health of body and the peace of mind of the working people in this country that they had ever seen—he meant the Insurance Act. (Applause.) Dr Macnamara declared that, despite the snarling of the political dogs in the manger, at the end of nine weeks the smoothness, the ease, and the readi- ness with which that great machine had been started and continued to run had exceeded his most ardent expectations. (Hear, bear.) It had been said that by that patriotic measure Mr Lloyd George had ruined the fortunes of the Liberal party. They would see at the end of twelve months, but whether it was so or not, it had vastly improved the fortunes of the State, and that ought to appeal even to Toryism. (Hear, hear.) He looked forward with the greatest confidence to the opeßation of the Act.

div.head: COST OF LIVING IN ONTARIO.
div.p: COST OF LIVING IN ONTARIO.

It is a widespread belief that the cost of living in Ontario is much higher than in Great Britain. Nothing can be further from the truth, as the following prices of farm products on the Toronto market last week will show :—Butter, Is Id per lb. ; eggs, Is Id per dozen ; pure native honey, 5d per lb. The prices for poultry were even lower than they are in Great Britaip ; spring chickens can be bought at 8d per lb. ; ducks, 6d per lb; turkeys, 9d per lb., and so forth. Fruit and vegetables are likewise at low prices, is., for instance for a basket of peaches, and Is Gd for a bushel of tomatoes, it will thus be seen that the purse of the housewife will go as far, if not farther, than it will in this country. The latest mail brings information that the Norfolk Fruit Growers' Association, which comprises the leading fruit growers in Norfolk County, Ontario, has disposed of the entire crop, consisting of about 50,000 bushels to one purchaser. This is the result of co-operation which is very strong in that county. By this aystem farmers ' are able to sell their crops at a minimum cost.

div.head: WHEAT AND FLOUR IMPORTS.
div.p: WHEAT AND FLOUR IMPORTS.
..... CANADA, OUR Mosr RELIABLE SOURCE OF SUPPLY. . _

At the Dundee meetincoitho British Association, Mr. R. 11. Rew's illuminating paper on agricultural statistics dealt with the question of the food supplies of the United Kingdom, from which it appears that. contrary to the current opinion on the subject, the value of food produced in the United Kingdom, exclu- sive of such articles as sugar, tea, coffee and cocoa, represents more than one half of the total food con- sumption of these islands. Of special interest are Mr. Rew's figures in regard to our eypenditure upon wheat and flour which is immense, and averages a little more thanone million sterling a week. The consumption works out at no less than =lbs. wheat per head. Practically jour-fifths of the total consumption, or 41 millions sterling, comes from abroad, against 10 millions sterling worth grown at home. Mr Rew says that wheat exports of the Empire last year would have been more than sufficient to supply the needs of the United Kingdom, but they were not all sent here. We received only 18 per cent. from British possessions. It appears that during the year Canada sent abrosd more wheat than any other country in the world. India Mr. Rew regards as the most uncertain source of imperial supply, although in good years it is one of the most formidable contri- butors to the wheat imports of the country. On the other hand Canada has shown itself to be our most trustworthy source of supply. During the last five years Canada has furnished 13.1 per cent, of the total consumption of wheat and flour of the United Kingdom as against Australia's 7.5 per cent.,lndia 10.5 per cont. and other British possessions 0.3 per cent. For the same period the United States supplies averaged 19.4 per cent, and the Argentine 14.8 per cent. In 1911 the United States percentage fell to 14.2, and Mr. Rew adds that " the United bitates must be regarded as a diminishing exporter,"
"THE STEAM BARGE, OR NAUTICAL NOVELTY."

A Glasgow correspondent, after reading the article by "AM." on the Centenary of the Steamship, sends us the followirg poem. It was written by William Muir, a saddler in Kirkintillcck, in March 1803. In that year a steamer was made which drew two loaded vessels along a canal. This is how the poet celebrated the event. His closing :lines- show considerable foresight.

When first by labour Forth an' Clyde Were taught o'er Scotia's hills to ride In a canal, deep, lang, and wide, Naebody thocht That winders, without win' or tide, Would o'er be wrocht. To gar them true that boats would sail Thro' fields o' corn or beds o' kail, Au' turn o'er glens their rudder's tail, Like weather-pocks, Was doctrine that wou'd needed bail Wl' common folks. They ca'd it nonsense, till at last They saw boats travel East and West, Wl' sails an' streamers at thair mast, Syne, without jeering, They were convinced the blustering blast Was worth the hearing. For mony a year, wi' little clatter, An' naething said about the matter, The horses haul'd them through the water Free Forth tee Clyde, Or the reverse, wi' weary splatter An' sweaty hide. Then we believed, poor silly bodies, Wha nathing ken o' Named studies, That hoses' hoofs and hempen woodies Be't still to draw them, An' cursing callens clad in dudies To swear end oa' them. But little think we what's in noddlee Whar science sits an' grapes an' god lea, Sjne darklins forth free drumly puddles Brings things to view That the weak penetration fuddles 0' me an' you. For lately we ha'e seen a Liehter, An' in her doup a Fanner fighter May bid bost-haulors gae digbt her Black sooty vent, Then half-a-dozen horse she'd wighter By ten per cent.

Wl' something that the learned ca' steam, That drives at heughts the wa'ken' beam 0' huge engines to draw coal seam Or carry hutches, She in her breast swells sic a feum As has few matches. By it through the water plashes, Sin' out the stream behint her dashes At sic a rate, baith frogs and fishes Are fore'd to scud Like ducks and drakes amang the rashes To shun the mud.

When first I saw her in a tether Draw two sloops after ace anither Regardless o' the win' an' weather Athwart her bearin', I thocht free hell she had come hither A privateerin% An' that the pair she had in tow Were prizes, struck me sae, I vow, I cried, when fixed to their prow I saw her cable, "In Satan's furnace noo they'll low Amang the rabble." It was odd to see her pulling, Au' win' an' weather baith unwilling. Yet dell-ma-care she onward sculling Defy'd them baith As constant as a mill that's fullin' Gude English chat). Can e'er, thought I, a flame )' reek, Or boiling water's cauldron smeek, Tho' it war keepit for a week, Perform sic wonders, As quite surprises must the folks 0' gazin' hunders.

But facts we canna weel dispute them, Altho' we little ken about them, When prejudice inclines to doubt them, WI, a' her might, Plain demonstrations chop can root them An' set us right. Or lang gae now wi' whirligigs An' steam engines we'll plough our rigs, An' gang about on easy legs; Wi' nought to pain us, But flit in tether needless nags That us'd to hain us.
Draw news indeed for man and beast ; They'll then ha'e nought to do but rest, An' on their former labours feast Wi' cheerful hearts, When thus they se warm steam insist To play their parts,

THE SCENE OF DEVASTATION AT CARDEN HALL, NEAR CHESTER, AFTER THE GREAT FIRE

A striking picture of Carden Hall after the fire had done its terrible work on Monday. The photograph brings home to the reader's mind the intensity of the blaze and the hopeless task of the firemen who hastened to the scene in answer to the summons. Priceless relics were consumed, and the various estimates of the damage utterly fail to convey to the mind the loss sustained by Colonel and Mrs. Holdsworth. [Manchester Courier Photo.

WOMEN'S CHAT.

Marriage Equality.—lt is thought that France will shortly follow the example of Switzerland, and delete the word " obedience " from the marriage service, as "by law established." Since the beginning of this year the marriage ceremony in Switzerland has omitted the promise "to obey" on the part of the wife, and there is a greater disposition in that country than in others to recognise the equality of the parties irdi matrimonal alliance. The menage is no longer a monarchy under the despotism of a single law giver, hut a republic, a mutual association founded on common interests and agreement. The Swiss law now recognises the right of the wife to an equal share of parental authority con- cerning the education and religious instruction of the children, who, at the age of sixteen can do as they like In such matters. There is little doubt, that sooner or later, the marriage ceremony in Western Europe will come to be generally reformed, so as to omit the vow "to obey." Feminine opinion is by no means unani- mous on this subject, for there is many a woman who likes to think her husband a superior being to herself. She is however free to do that, %bother the promise is made or not, and the words aro really superfluous in the marriage contract, as it is nowadays regarded both by the law and modern sociat.conditions. _ _ _ . .

The Perfect Spouse.—The editor of an American newspaper seems to think that the State ought to set up a standard of efficiency for husbands and wives. His own wife apparently thinks he has many of the faults charged against husbands generally, and in order to prove that he is as good as most husbands, he offered a substantial prize for the Perfect Spouse. His wife, choosing the most likely cases, has been beating up her friends, to enter their husbands for the competition, and it remains to be seen whether the editor will gain his point in showing that the perfect husband does not exist. Not long ago, Mrs. Anna Murphy, chief police matron of Chicago, offered some advice on choosing a husband. "Big men "she said make the best husbands. In her opinion they are easiest to get along with ; are less irritable, and more generous than the little man, who is likely to be nervous and iflgety. A man of small stature, with a sharp thin nose, she rays is apt to be a scold, and a fault tinder. Mrs. Murphy's views conflict with the opinion of most physiognoinists that biz fat men are usually selfish but her official duties, no doubt, enable her to speak • with some authority on these matters. The Public Milk Supply.—The Legislature has still to deal with some important aspects of the public milk supply, but the new regulation of the Local Govern- ment Board which comes into operation in Eugl ail and Wales, on October Ist, will make it illegal for any dealer to use chemicals for preserving milk or cream. This is a step which will be welcomed, especially on behalf of young children and invalids, whose health, or perhaps life, depends upon a dietary of pore, whole- some, and undrugged milk. Many of the principal dairies have long since given up the use of preservatives, and now adopt the pasteurisation system, which con- sists of heating the milk up to NO degrees, and then cooling it rapidly down to 40 degrees. The necessary plant for this process is however, expensive, and there is no doubt that the alternative—the Use of preservi- tives—is still very generally resorted to. Many medical men attribute the prevalence of appendicitis to the widespread use of chemicals as food preservatives, 11:.d the prohibition with regard to milk should bs all to the good as Jegards the publio health. Nor should it be harmful to the milk dealers as the fact that the Importation of foreign milk, which does not comply with the new regulation is prohibited, is obviously good for the home trade. Autumn Fashione.—The autumn season of 1912 bids fair to prove cf exceptional interest from the point of view of fashions and colours.The influence of Directoire styles—for these must be !poken of in the plural—is apparent not only in the cut-away basque, end the coat that contrasts with the skirt, but in neckwear and the arrangement of collars. The contrasting coat, a simple

tailored garment, will be seen more e,pecially with the pleated skirt. The three piece dress, consisting of hodice, skirt and coat, is distinctly gaining in favour, and hero again, the coat may be of a different fabric from the dress. Thus a complete dress of velveteen may have a coat of cloth. Narrow skirts will remain in favour, although pleats in a variety of forms are- seen, and draperies will be very discreetly introduced on some tailored gowns. Concerning Colours.—With regard to colours, it is interesting to note the radical change that has of late years been wrought in the sentiment of women in this connection. Years ago,certain colours were impossible ; now all colours, and their combinations, are permitted. Many women make a study of colours, and having arrived at one that suits them, use it freely, scarcely troubling whether it is fashionable or not. In the coming season, rich, warm tones will predominate, and as they are invariably becoming to the woman who is no longer young, will be sure of a warm welcome. Blues in soft tones, mulberry, dahlia, Bordeaux, purple, warm shades of brown, and reds, from pale pink to crimson, ' not omitting yellow, ti,at has been so much worn this summer, are all to have their devotees. The Blanket CAA —There are unmistakeable signs that the Blanket Cost in blue will be much more popular this winter than in the reversible cloths that were so universally worn last year, and this notwith- standing the effarls of designers and others to brighten the monotony of our streets by the introduction of vivid colours, in out-door raiment generally. Heavy cloths with a serge-like surface and a wide rib loik very well iu blue, which is not only a homely and serviceable colour, but very convenient also. It is said that ,the stranger arriving on our shores sees so many women garbed in blue serge or cloth in the street; that ho comes to the rather hasty conclusion that we never wear light or bright colours. New Petticoate.—Yetticoats are coming back to I favour again, and nothing but praise can b 3 accorded to I the new shapes—which fit like a glove to the knees, where they flare out slightly tt) the hem. On the sides nearer the back than the front the seams are cut with what may be termed extensions. These are pleated and pressr•cl very flat, making no perceptible difflrence to the silhouette, yet they give width at the hem, since they open when the wearer walks. Picturesque Hosiery.—Short skirts and low shoes, are answerable for the increase and multiplication of picturesque designs in stockings. A new design resembles a draught board, being in large squares, another is reminiscent of a barber's pole, with its winding ribbons of bright colours. Not one, but many colours and shades wind round the ankle of the new hosiery in curved diagonal lines. Paris is showing stockings made of real gold and silver thread, of which 3 tissue is formed. The effect is beautiful, but naturally they are very expensive. In America fashion- able women are wearing odd stockings, one being white another black, a fashion that will not be likely to find I favour on this aide of the Atlantic. -

Muffs and Neck Furs.— the fashionably dressed woman is to be very " furriery " this coming autumn and winter, and muffs composed of several different furs will be of more mammoth size than ever. The woman who aims at the sensational may be trusted to make the most of this vogue, but it is a matter .for regret that what was once a comfort and a necessity. •houll be transformed by a freak of fashion into an absurdity and a burden. The furriers are, of course, chiefly responsible for this, and by every means at their command they cultivate the taste for a lavish display of peltry. Whilst the silk and woollen manufacturers are lamenting a falling off of business, owing to the hobble skirt tnode, the fur trade is rej icing in busy and prosperous times. The shops are showing various original little fitments for the neck, in the guise of high sto-...k5, P.)bewierre c3llars and cravats—and the ihort neck fur, with head, is sure to he very popular.
