Sir Henry Hibbert presided over Monday's meeting of the Lancashire Education Committee at Preston. . _

Mr .1 J Cockehott, in presenting the elementary education report, said it was desirable to have an inter- view with the officials of the Board of Education on certain questions raised in a letter from the Board dated May 1 with reference to the arrangements for carryiug out the work of school medical inspection in the county area. In that latter it was stated that the arrange- ments in Lancashire for the examination of defective eyesight and hearing and the clinical work of the assistant medical officers were above the average, but that the system of inspection was open to criticism. The circular of April 9 divided the work of medical inspection into three parts. One was medical inspec- tion proper, where the Committee's system, though ,not strictly in accordance with the Board's schedule, was more effective than the Board's plan. To comply with the desire of the Board they should have to expend immediately a capital sum of about £2,5000 and should have to add £3,000 a year ta their permanent expendi- ture on the school medical department. They wished therefore to discuss with the Board whether it was necessary that they should incur that expenditure. The advice of the Committee's o All school medical snperiu• tendent was that their present system was adequate. The second part was work associated with medical treatment. The Committee had done a good deal of that kind of work tip to the present time, and he was not sure it would be necessary for them to incur any great expense in complying with the Board's require- ments in that particular. But the Government had placed at the disposal of the Board £OO,OOO for grants to local education authorities in aid of expenditure for medical treatment. The Committee had done practically I nothing in the way of medical treatment Veyond encouraging the pareuts to get children treated o.6cord- ing to the advice given after inspection. If the £60,000 were divided pro rata according to the number of children in the schools, the Committee's] share would be about £1,600. The question they had to consider was whether their present arrangements, under which a good deal of medical treatment was obtained volun- tarily, ought to be superseded by a more compelling system, under which they would no doubt have to pro- vide for various expenditure, in order that they might get a share of the £60,000 a year. Ile had read that in 1907, out of 2,000 young men presenting themselves in Manchester to enter the Army, upwards of 1,000 werel rejected as physically unlit. How far they, acting as an education authority, could remedy such a state of things was a matter which would require very careful consideration. Ile thought that when the deputation returned they would be able to place some scheme before the committee which would satisfy the Board of Education and at the same time not impose on the I ratepayers a greater burden than was absolutely , necessary. The report was adopted.

WARNING FROM INSURANCE COMMISSIONERS The Health Insurance Commission (England) point out that insured persons must either join an approved society before October 2Cah, or become deposit contributors, and that societies if approved after that date would be unlikely to secure any substantial num- b3r of members for State Insurance. Owing to the heavy pressure which is certain to arise at the end of the current quarter, the commissioners cannot hold out any prospect of granting approval during this quarter to societies who have nt yet made formal application, unless their rules are forwarded without delay, and at the latest by Saturday next.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
THE DEADLY HATPIN.

11 Yes, as previously remarked in an editoral note, there are ladies who persist in going to and fro in our midst wearing headgear bristling with formidable pins that constantly menace unwary passers-by. Several minful and irreparable mishaps have cccurred as direct results of this extreme carelessness. lam con- vinced the time is not distant when such folly will be openly denounced as criminal recklessness. The thoughtless perpetrators are quite without excuse, for as they must know well enough, articles are now obtainable, whereby the dangerous mints may be effectually protected. They are supplied in various sizes and patterns to match the ornamental heads of the pins, and are now worn by all ladies who have any regard for their own reputations and who recognise their grave responsibility. I fear, however, that those who stand most in need of such reasonable precautions arc just the persons who will rush on their perilous way, leaving their inoffensive and long- suffering fellow-creatures to guard their own eyes and what not.

"WHAT ABOUT HUDDERSFIELD ? " An old dame who was a more devout than intelli- gent reader of the Scriptures gratefully testified that she had long been accustomed to derive comfort and inspiration from that blessed word "Mesopotamia." The reader has heard of her often. I have myself found "Huddersfield " a blessed word; but to utter it in the bearing of the member for Warrington has come to be somewhat of a risky experiznent. I wonder if the example of the French candidate for honours similar to those now enjoyed by Mr Harold would be of any use to that harassed and rather irritable ' gentleman. He was a very distinguished man in various other walks of life, but did not make a good candidate when the voice of the heckler was heard in the land. Once, when delivering a learned harangue he was interrupted with —"Ah,but what about Madagascar ? " He could not think at the moment of any crisis or particular trouble affecting Madagascar, so he proceeded to draw upon his encyclormic knowledge of the island in question and the inhabitants thereof. At a subsequent meeting in another part of the con- stituency the same unknown voice struck in with— " Yes, but what about Madagascar? " Again the perplexed speaker, convinced that there was something about Madagascar that he ought to know and did not, sought to throw dust in the eyes of his interrupter and to impress the general body of hearers by holding forth solemnly upon the island's trade and prospects—in fact, he dragged in all he could think of respecting it. fie afterwards button- holed the heckler in private, and asked what he meant by following him from place to place and reiterating that troublesome question about Madagascar " Well you see, sir," the fellow explained, "I intend to emigrate to Madagascar and to go into business there ; but I wanted first to find out all that was possible about it, and I was satisfied you could give me more information on the subject than any other man, so I kept at it till I'd pumped you fairly dry! " Here's a tip for Mr Harold when he's next asked— What about Huddersfield ? " Let him simply assume that his questioner wants a descrip!ion of the leading features of the place. Said a stranger to an old Irish fishwife, indicating one after another of the cuts on her stall : "How much is this a pound? And this, and this, and that "—" Arrab, be done wid yer," was the ultimate retort; "sure, it's not fish ye want, it's information." Well, that's what some of us are still thirsting for respecting Huddersfield ; and who so likely to impart it as the present member for Warrington ? PRISONERS IN CANAL.

Last week's Court case at Daresbury, in which it was stated that a tramp had temporarily eluded arrest for begging by assaulting a constable and then swimming across the canal, reminded me of a story which John Hartley, the Yorkshire dialect writer, with whom I happen to be personally acquainted, used to tell many years ago.. It .was to the effect that two young fellows were sitting.in a field corner gaming with dominoes, when a police officer, concealed by the wall, managed to get near .enough to hear all that passed between the pair. During a pause, the one asked the other, "Can't ta come Tom?" Immediately, the constable popped up with-.." I can come." The two mates at once took to their heels, but as they ran in different directions, of course the officer could only follow one. The youth he was pur- suing headed straight for the canal. and unhesitatingly plunged in, He gained the opposite bank in safety,

and then, turning towards the crestfallen man in blue, impudently jeered—" Can't ta come, policeman?" Some years ago, a certain PS. Edmondson of my acquaintance apprehended a desperate criminal on a charge of burglary in a district in which I was then stationed. As they went along the road together, the prisoner pretended that he had hidden the " swag" in a wall oa the canal Bide, and induced his custodian to take him on to the towing path for the purpose of recovering the stolen jewellery. As soon as they got near the \rater, the fellow suddenly broke away and dived in. For once, however, he had reckoned with- out his host. Edmondson was a noted athlete, and, being an excellent swimmer, fearlessly followed the accused, and, seizing him in the water, soon had biro roaring for mercy and promising him to " go quietly." Ile then dragged his prisoner out, and although there still remained a four-mile walk to the police station, the fellow gave no more trouble. AN AMUSING ERROR.

In the course of his address on "The ideal of a Free Church," Dr. Mellor took occasion to comment upon the consistent and persistent avoidance of doctrinal tests throughout the long history of the Cairo-street Church. The reference brought to my mind a laughable incident which Caine under my notice two or three years ago. The vicar of the parish in which I then resided, spoke from the pulpit on " Why have ' a creed ? " and a young reporter on one of the local papers informed readers in the following issue that the topic dealt with by the rev gentleman, was " Why have a Queen? " Naturally, the worthy cleric, whose loyalty is unquestionable, was much annoyed ; indeed from what he said to me afterwards, he wal feeling just at the moment that the wretch who had committed the awful blunder deserved "something with boiling oil in it." INSURANCE OF CASUALS.

I rather suspect there are casual workers who would be ready to aid and abet adverse critics at the other end of the social scale in visiting some such clrast c punishment upon the devoted author of the Insurance Act. The other day a relative of mine endeavoured to make terms with a charwoman who had served her on some previous occasions. The irsurance business proved a stumbling block. " Well," said the woman, "I'll come, but I won't ha one o' them there cards." To be sure, in cases where the charwoman raises no such objection but accepts the inevitable, it is possible and is becoming more and more common for employers to arrange to pay the weekly contribution in turn. THE WEATHER.

The abnormally wet season, as to which at last a welcome break has occurred, recalled how in the visitors' book at the White Lion Hotel, Bala, Or. Walsharp How, first Bishop of Wakefield, many years before his death wrote thus ;
"The weather depends on the moon as a rule, And we found that the toying is true ; For at Data it rains when the moon's at the full, And it rains when the moon's at the new.

When the moon's at the quarter then down comes the rain, At half it's no better I wean; When the moon's at three•quarters it's at it again, And besides it rains mostly between." This in turn reminds me of an equally good one which I somehow fancy was penned by Mrs. Humphry Ward, though as to that I may be mistaken. I came across it several years ago, but it is quite short and I can easily repeat it from memory. Here it is "The rain it raineth every day Upon the just and unjust fellows; But more upon the just because The unjust have the justs' umbrellas." FLAG-FLYING. " Union Jack " interposes a timely protest against the mistaken local habit of retaining flags in position, night and day, when once they are hoisted on public buildings. He might, while be was about it, have added an objection to being occasionally left-standing on his head. Now and then the National emblem is hoisted by persons who are apparently unaware that the Union Jack has a right and a wrong side, and they accidentally float it wrong, way up ! In that position, of course, it signifies something altogether different from the sentiment which the well-meaning promoters intend to convey. It is just as well "to think on these things."
FOU ND. THE GLAD EYE--and It was Mother's. No wonder she was pleased. She had just proved what a blessing Steedman's Powders are to Parents. Nothing else keeps children so fit.

Great Sankey. CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE.—About eighty members of the Warrington Church Lads' Brigade were present at divine service at St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey on Sunday morning. They marched from Warrington to the church under the command of Lieut.-Col. F. M. Appleton, and were accompanied by the bugle band. The Vicar (hey. J. R. Jones) occupied the pulpit, and preached from the text "Thou hest given a banner to them that fear Thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth," Psalm lx. 4. Special hymns were sung, Miss Standish was at the organ.

Lymm. ATIDDLEWICII Snow Wissart.—We notice that Mrs John Merrill of High Legh has followed up her successful exhibits of butter at the Mid-Cheshire and Wirral shows by taking the second prize at the Middle- wich Show held on Wednesday.

, - PRESENTATION TO M. P. LEATHER.—The teachers and scholars who were at the afternoon session of the Congregational Sunday School on the 15th inst., were the witnesses of an interesting presentation. On behalf of the members of the Sunday School and Christian Social Service Band Mr J H Holt presented to„.Mr P N Leather, in connection with his recent marriage (as reported in our last issue) a set of table cutlery. Mr Holt in making the sresentation spoke of Mr P N Leather's excellent services amongst them and wished him and his wife much happiness in their future lite. Mr Leather replied in a suitable manner. PRIMITIVE METHODIST HARVEST FF.STICAL.—The local Primitive Methodist body are usually the first in the district to hold their harvest festival services, and in accordance with this tradition these were celebrated on Sunday and Monday last. The decoration of the church, which was left in the bands of Mrs Whiteway ; the Misses Smith, Welford, 13 Cr' oss Eva Tone, and M E Tongs; and Messrs A Appleton, 61 Appleton, hi Clare, G Cross, J Edwards and A B Edwards, Was tastefully executed, the white and green decorations at the front of the choir seats, pulpit, reredos, and back window forming a pleasing effect. Considering the season there was a good show of flowers, fruit. and vegetables. The preacher on Sunday waerthe Rev P H Horner, who came in the place of the Rev Ford, who was uniortunately too ill to fulfil the engagement. There was a good attendance at the morning service, but at night the church was packed. Mr Ilorner chose as his text" The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few." He spoke about the harvest and Christ's compassion on the multitude, and His appeal for labourers to work in the ready harvest which appeared before Him. After dwelling on Christ's faith in humanity, he showed bow that a great harvest was now ready for attention in the form of doing away with militarism, white slave traffic, slums and drunkenness, and that Christ was calling for men to enter His service. The choir gave an excellent rendering of Edmund Turner's anthem "Great and marvellous.' On Monday evening there was a good attendance to bear the choir give an able interpretation of the service of song entitled "The Master of Wychelm Farm " (A J Jamouneau.) Miss M J Appleton pleasantly sang the solo "The last call," while Mr H Clare was successful with the tenor solo " Tares and corn." The two quartettes were taken by the Misses E Appleton. D Cross and Messrs J Atherton, 0 Appleton, H Clare and G Cross. Mr U L Welford gave a clear reading of the narrative and at the close of the piece commented on the excellent manner in which the music had been rendered. He tendered his thanks to all who had brought gifts to the Festival and said that he believed they had done right in holding the services, despite the many remarks that had been made against thanksgiving services this year, as he was confident that they had many things to he thankful for. Mr .1 Edwards was the conductor and Miss Shore the organist. The produce was afterwards disposed of in the schoolroom when Mr Warham executed the duties of salesman. The financial result was slightly in advance ot last year's total. CLERKS AND THE INSURANCE ACT —Under the auspices of the National Amalgamated Union of Shop Assistants, Warehousemen and Clerks, a meeting was held in Hurst's Pavilion on Thursday night for the pur- pose of forming a new branch as an Approved Society under the National Insurance Act. Mr Piercey in taking the chair stated his pleasure at being present and defined the purpose of the gathering. Mr H H Duke, one of the Union's Organisers,was the principal speaker of the evening. He outlined the object, working and benefits of the Society. He said that amongst other things the Society had obtained for shop assistants were the half day holiday, specific hours for meals, and the withdrawal of " Radius Agreements " that affected between four and five thousand shop managers. Whilst expressing his gratitude for these improvements be said that the Union still ' desired reform in relation to—early closing, sanitation and ventilation of business premises, abolishment of fines and the living-in system. It was the desire of the union to keep unemployment registers so as to assist members who were out of work, to regulate the under- standing between masters and men, and to give mem- bers legal aid. Mr. Duke strongly denounced Insurance Companies' Approved Societies and claimed that if for only the two following reasons his Society was the better :—(1) Being worked chiefly by voluntary workers they had not to pay so much money away in salaries. (2) On the whole shop assistants were a healthy class and had not to take such risks as persons in many other trades and as only persons in the dis- tributive trades were eligible for membership the union's risks and calls e ere less. They were expecting therefore that when the triennial valuation was made that they would have sufficient surplus money as to be able to extend medical benefits not only to the worker, but to those dependent upon that worker : Free dental treatment. Found an old-age pension fund. Apart from these mercenary benefits the union was an asset to the members' social life, many forms of entertainment being given at the branches in both winter and summer. Alas as the Union bad branches in different parts of the country they were able to assist members who had removed from one town to another. Special benefits were provided for lady members. For these reasons he believed that his society was the best and so he appealed for new members. Mr HoAson, the secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of the Union endoreed Mr Duke's remarks and spoke at length on the subject of" Radius Agreements" and gave examples of cases he knew where the Union had assisted members in times of oppression. The election of officers for tbe Lymm branch was then proceeded with and resulted as follows :—Chairman' Mr Piercey ; vice-chairman, Mr Blount ; secretary, Mr Spencer ; treasurer, Mr Driver. Mr Duke wished the new branch every success. LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.

They sent a letter in which they recorded their objection to the Act and offered to pay under protest. The summonses were withdrawn.

div.head: RIFLE SHOOTING.
div.p: RIFLE SHOOTING.

Appleton Club's Success at Liverpool. Members of the Appleton Rifle Club figured with gratifying success in the fifth annual championship meet ing of the Liverpool Miniature Rifle Association, at the Liverpool City Police Rifle Club's range, on Saturday. In the championship competition the second prize, which is the Oldfield Cup and Association silver medal was secured by Mr E Pollard with a score of 230 out of a possible 300, being only one point behind the winner of the" Courier" and " Express" Challenge Cup, Mr A Sruy, of the Bootle Police Force. The sth prize was won by Mr A Shepherd, with the score of 286; the 9th by Mr C P Day, with a score of 283, and the 25th by MrFC Bennion with a score of 973. In the inexpert competition the first prize, a case of cutlery, was won by Mr S James, with a score of 281 out of a possible 300. Mr C liennion won the special 'prize offered by the Society of Miniature Rifle Clubs for the best score made by an inexpert with a S.M.R.C. converted Martini rifle, with a score of 275 out of a possible 300. The club also secured the Pichards ChallengeCtm, beating Liverpool Municipal Rifle Club in the final. In this competition the prize is won by the team who break first five discs of two inches diameter at NO yards range. Appleton accomplished the task in the final in 25 seconds. The successful team consisted of Messrs A Shepherd, C P Day, E Pollard and S Jones.
The Examiner, Saturday, September 21, 1912.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
FALL FROM A WAGGONETTE. BEER AND FOOTBALL.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens on Monday on William Swift, French polisher, of 204, Elephant-lane, who died during Saturday night alter falling out of a waggonette in which he had visited Runcorn to witness the football match between St. Helens and Runcorn. George Swift, his brother, said that the waggonette left the Red, White and Blue public-house about two o'clock on Saturday afternoon. They had beer before they started, some more on the way, and after the foot- ball match they returned to Widnes and strolled about. About eight o'clock they left Widnes, and they arrived at St. Helens at 11.10 p.m , when Swift, in getting out of the waggonette, jumped and fell, his head striking the top of a postal letter-box and his skull being frac- tured. Witness complained bitterly that he was unable to get a doctor, and said that at the different places at which he called he was treated like a dog and not as an Englishman. The Coroner : Well, I see that it took you from eight o'clock until 11.10 to get from Widnes to St. Helens. I know the district, and I could have walked it in that time.

Witness : Yes, sir. The Coroner : I expect you had some beer. Witness: I was quite capable. I came to the police office at 1.30, and an inspector who spoke to me would have locked me up if I had been drunk. Inspector Dunn said that the man came to tbe office, and the officers in charge had a lot of trouble with him because he was in a drunken condition. Another witness complained that when they went to the relieving officer to ask him to get a doctor he listened to them and then shut the window in their faces. The Coroner said they must take that up with the guardians. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." CHEQUES AND CHANGE. ALLEGED FRAUDS AT ST. HELENS.

William Hall, alias Barnes. &c.,who had been brought to the court by a warder from Blackburn Gaol, was on Monday charged at St. Helens with obtaining two sums of money by false pretences. The evidence was that on Friday, July 19th, the prisoner called at the _house of Alfred Hayes, painter, of 209, Park-road, and said he had come to the district wit' l four men to build a bridge and wanted lodgings for them. Mrs. Hayes agreed to take them in. On the Saturday and Sunday Hall borrowed 4s, and on the Monday got 3s in order to wire for his tools. As security for the money Hall, who at that time stated that his name was John Forest, gave Mrs Hayes a stamped piece of paper which, he said, was a note for £6 4s. He then disappeared, and the paper was found to be worthless. He had since been arrested and committed for trial at Blackburn on another charge. Detective-inspector Dunn said the prisoner had no work at St Helens at the time spoken to. When charged with the offence he said, "I know the cheque, and I plead guilty to the charge." In the second case, the prisoner went on Friday June 28th, to the furniture shop of Charles Wood, 114, Liverpool-road and by means of a cheque made some purchases and got change, which represented the difference between the full value of the cheque and the purchase price. He said to the person in. charge, " I suppose you take cheques ? If you have a bank you can cash it, but I have not. I got it for some work I have done." He gave the name of John Wilson, and said be li•ed at Denton's Green, and had got the cheque from a Mr. Harrison, pawnbroker, of Liverpool. The man gave orders for the goods to be sent to an address in Liver- pool, but found that the cheque and address were bogus. Prisoner was committed for trial at the assizes.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.

WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION (N.A. CENTRE). Owing to the great improvement in the weather, members were out in great numbers last week-end. Norton was visited on Thursday, Saturday and Sunday. The Gowy also had visitors on the Saturday, but the card of the week was the annual match at Hartford. We are now getting close to the time when the set board closes for the year 1912 and unless the specimen hunters do better than they have been doing this last few weeks they will have to look to the;r laurds. The match season is practically over, and if fine weather continues members who only interest themselves in match fishing may go in for the heavier specimens and they have not a great deal to beat, except in the roach column.

div.head: ANNUAL MATCH.
div.p: THE ANNUAL MATCH.

The match that has been looked forward to for some weeks turned out a success, as the committee antici- pated. Even the weather was kind to the Association for the first time in five years on annual match day. Members met at headquarters at 8 a m. on Sunday last to travel by motor to Hartford, but owing to a delay it was 9.15 when a start was made, and the two cars made a good run to Stretton, when a short halt was called. Members here were counted up, and we found 50 was the number, the remainder going by bike or train. After consulting our watches we tound with a fair run, we would have an hour to get ready for the match, which proved correct, several trying their luck before coming up to draw ; one member taking a line perch that drew the scale at 9ozs. 3drms. This in the contest would have lauded him well amongst the first six. The draw took place at 12.15 and the contest was well on at 12.45 Messrs Stout and Potter having little trouble in getting the 63 anglers in position and seeing everyone fixed up right. After the word " all in " was given, number 60 had landed in the first half minute, and this was the only one he had got during the contest. Numbers were called now and again but it was soon to be seen that the member who could weigh a Sib when time was called would not be far-off the winner. Fish in number were taken but they were of the poorest class seen at Hartford for some time. One member caught eleven roach for a little over 40z. Hoe ever, when time was called the weighers selected got to business without delay. Messrs Potter and Taylor started from No. 1 and Messrs Stout and Hamblett from 63 and meeting somewhere near centre. When notes were compared we found 14' Jolley the winner with lib sdrs, E Hill running him very close with 15oz 15drs. Jolley indeed had to work hard to win as he broke several lashes daring the contest and a novice in his peg would have had little chance of bang returned the winner. ---------

Out of 63 anglers 34 weighed W course more than the 34 caught fish, but they was such small stuff that the anglers thought that their weight would have no chance of being in the prizes, thus several threw their chance away. Thirty prizes for thirty four that weighed in must be a recordland we have great pleasure in again thanking our donors for making the match the success of the season. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. . . _

The prize distribution took place at headquarters, Gladstone Arms. on Tuesday last, over forty members putting in appearance. Mr. Ellison officiated in the absence of the Chairman of the society who was unable to attend. After a few remarks on the progress of the club he called up the Ist prize winner at 8.10 p.m., the , Ist, 2nd and 3rd winners coming in for great applause.' All the prizes were given out by 9 p.m., then followed a few remarks by members on the way the society had carried out its business, members all rising to drink success to the club. A musical programme was contri- buted to by Messrs. Richards, Sherratt, Taylor, Stout, Simcock, Ellison, Bryers, and Darhyshire. The tit-bit of the evening was Its a funny little place to have one" sung by 3. Derbyshire, and causing much amuse- ment amongst the anglers.l

div.head: COUNTY REVISION COURTS.
div.p: COUNTY REVISION COURTS.
STOCKTON HEATH.

The annual revision of the voters' lists for the Knutsford Division of Cheshire has been conducted this week by Mr. Clement Elphinstone Lloyd. On Wednesday morning he attended at the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, to revise the lists for the Appleton, Stockton Heath and Grappenhall polling districts. Mr H Cliffe represented the Liberals and Mr G Duckworth appeared on behalf of the Conservatives. The follow- ing assistant overseers were present :—Stockton Heath, Mr Edwin Bradshaw ; Appleton and Stratton, Mr John Ellison ; Grappenball, Mr C H Iloult ; Latchford Without, Mr Joseph Smith ; Lower Walton, Mr H Lawrence (also representing Mr W H Woodcock, assistant overseer for Warringtcn) ; Walton Superior, Mr A Moulsdale.

WEEK'S BREAK IN TENANCY LOSES VOTE. Jr Cliffe claimed an occupiers' vote for Peter Cliffs!, Cawdor-street, Stockton Heath. He said Mr Cliffe left the house and went to live in Warrington for one week. He, however, left some goods in the house and the con- tention was that the tenancy was therefore continuous. Mr Duckworth said the tenancy was broken in the first week in January. When Mr Cliffe went to live in Warrington, be bad no intention of returning to Stockton Heath. However, the new house did not please him so a week later he went back to the house in Cawctor-street and took it again. During his absence the house had been let to someone else and Mr Cliffe had to make arrangements with the new tenant to get it hack again. Mr. Cliffe said the house was empty all the time. It was not a Question of whether the claimant left it for a week. He had the rent book to show a continuous tenancy. Mr. Duckworth said the claimant arranged with the new tenant to pay a week's rent in order to get the house back again. Mr. Bradshaw : That is so. The claimant left about January 3rd and went to Warrington. He found the new house was not suitable and came back. In the mean- time the landlord had let the house to another party and the condition on which the claimant was allowed to take the house a second time was that he should pay a week's rent. The vote was not allowed. OVERSEER CONGRATULATED. At the close of the revision of the list for Stockton Heath, the Revising Barrister said he bad pleasure in again congratulating Mr. Bradshaw on the excellence of the list. OWNERSHIP VOTE DISALLOWED. The ownership vote of Councillor C Jackson Holmes in respect of land at Latchford Without was objected to on the ground that he himself was the occupier of the land. Mr. Cliffe contended that the objection bad not been published. At any rate, it did not appear on the notice board. Mr Smith said that not only was the objection published but Councillor Jackson Holmes was person- ally informed of it. Mr Cliffs said he had to write to the assistant overseer three times for a list before he got a reply. Mr smith : I was informed by the postal authori- ties that the application was sent to we by halfpenny post, addressed to Tower View, a house which I left six years ago. It never reached me. Mr G Pilling, overseer for Latchford Without, gave evidence that the ownership list, together with the objections, had been duly published. Mr Smith : With regard to Mr Cliffs's remarks as to applying three times, the third application reached me, with tne observation of the postman that the others had been returned because they were addressed to Tower View.
The vote was disallowed. LODGER CLAIMS.

In the parish of Stockton Heath, the Conservatives claimed a lodger vote for Frank Mclntyre. Mr Chile objected on the ground that he had not separate occupation. The claim was not allowed. Joseph Sankey claimed a lodger vote and the Liberal agent again objected, as there were too many people living in the house. This WaR also struck out. Mr Cliffe objected to the lodger claim of Fred Timperley and the Barrister disallowed the vote. In the parish of Walton Inferior Mr 0 J Gregory was successful in claiming as a lodger voter, as were also Mr W H Grounds and Mr J T Picton, jun. The claims were supported by Mr Cliffe. The Liberal agent also supported the claim of Mr R Amos in the township of Warrington and the Barrister allowed the claim. A SAILOR'S VOTE.

There was considerable discussion as to the objection by the Conservatives, to the occupation vote of Jack T Dawson in Grappenball parish. The Liberal agent stated that Mr Dawson was a sailor and away on a voyage to Australia but that his wife still resided in tbe house. Mt, Duckworth strongly opposed the vote and said the ' house was empty. The Assistant Overseer informed the Barrister that he had seen the wife at the house and she was still residing there. Mr Cliff contended that as the voter was on the high seas on his Majesty's service and unable to appear, he ought to have the benefit of any doubt there might be. 'the objection failed and Mr DAWSOO was left on the list.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION.
PEN KETH.

The annual revision of the voters' lists for the town- ships or places of Bold, Cuerdley, Great Sansey, and Penketh was held at the Institute, Stocks-lane' Penketh, yesterday morning, by Mr C H Marriott Wharton, revising barrister. The following represented the political parties :—Messrs W A Mawdsley and J Noble (Conservatives), Mr W Forshaw (Labour), Mr F J Downes (Liberal.) The overseers present were :—Mr J Smith (Sankey), Mr E Forster (Periketh), Mr J Fair- dough (Bold), and Mr H B Wright (Cuerdley.) There were two lodger claims and one ownership claim for Bold ; one occupier's claim for Cuerdley ; two occupiers' claims for Sankey, and four ownership ; and four occupiers' claims and one lodger claim for Penketh Objections had been raised to four on the occupiers' list. Jabez Arthur West, The Mount, Penketh, claimed a lodger vote.—Mr Forster (overseer) pointed out that the gross value was £24 and £2l rateable. It was a large house, and applicant occupied a back Ledroom and front sitting-room. He was of the opinion it was a genuine lodger claim. The vote was allowed. An objection was raised to the occupier's vote of Ssdnev Atherton. Mr Maw dsley pointed out that Sarah Atherton was on the list last year. Mr Forshaw (Labour) : The o.,jection is bad. I have the rent books here to show applicant was the tenant. The objection was over-ruled. The name of Gilbert Marsh, 23, Back Gardens, Penketh, was struck off the list. Mr Mawdsley, the Conservative agent, said applicant had not resided in the house for the quail f ying period.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

hirWharton attended at theWarrington Police Station at noon yesterday, to revise the lists for Poulton-with- Fearnhead, Rixton-with-Glazebrook, Warrington and Woolston-with-Martinscroft. AGENTS NOT RECOGNIZED.

In one case in which an overseer said he had allowed a name to go on the list with the consent of the politi- cal agents, the Barrister remarked : You must not do anything with the consent of the agents. We don't recognise them at all. It is a great privilege for the 1 agents to come here.

div.head: AN OBJECTION AND A PROTEST.
div.p: AN OBJECTION AND A PROTEST.

Walter Podmore Ashton, 272, Manchester-road, War- ington, appeared to claim an ownership vote which was objected to by the Conservatives as well as by the overseers. Producing the Conservative notice of objection, which was signed by Harold Bingham, Mr Ashton remarked : I think I ought to protest against this objection in any case, whether the vote goes through or not. lam not in the habit of bringing claims forward unless IBM absolutely justified, and I think I am entitled to pro- test most strongly against it. Mr W II Woodcock (assistant overseer) said the objection of the overseers was that the qualification was not sufficiently definite. Mr Ashton was not known to them as the owner of freehold land in Manchester- road. Mr Ashton : The objection I protest against is the one I received by post, signed by Mr Harold Bingham, of Great Sankey. I don't know who he is. Mr Mawdsley : You have only received the same treatment as other claimants. Mr Ashton : I say nothing at all about that. The Barrister : This is a case where there was en objection by the overseer, which I suppose these people did not know anything about. Tney did not know the reason why he bad objected and I aupposiii they thought tbeY would be in too. Mr Ashton : I say nothing about] the overseers objection. That is quite in order. Mr Mawesley : This is a new claim nd it is usual to obj ect to first claims in order that the bona fides may be proved, Mr Ashton : This is the first time I have had the chance of putting in a claim for this vote, and I don't think Harold Bingham, whoever he nay be, has any more right than anyone elso to object it. I have been brought down here at considerable inconvenience, and I don't think the thing is straight and fair. Deeds were produced showing that Mr Ashton held the freehold of land, on which there were three dwell- ing-houses, in Manchester-road. The Barrister pointed out that there would have been no necessity for Mr Ashton to attend the Court if he
on hand, ready for immediate use, a box of

had given particulars to the assistant overseer at an earlier date. Mr Ashton : I felt very strongly when I got that notice. I thought it was bitting below the belt. If it is the accepted thing I have nothing further to say. The Barrister: Your vote is all right. Mr Ashton: I should not, have made a claim if I had not been sore of getting it. The Barrister pointed out that although he objected strongly to an all-round notice of objection, he had laid it down as his ruling that objections were permissible in cases where the claimant had not supplied all particulars to the overseer. Mr. Downes said be knew of twenty cases this sear which were not entitled to be on the register, but which would have been left on if objections had not been taken. Mr Ashton : What nettled me was that this was an absolutely bona fide claim in every detail. If I had bad a ghost of a chance in taking legal proceedings, I should have done so.

Mr Mawdsley : It is the legal form of objection. Mr Ashton : If it had not been, Bingham would have heard something shout it. Mr Downes : If Mr Bingham objects to you again, you will be able to claim heavy expenses. Mr Ashton : Quite right. I hope he will. (Laughter.) Is my vote in order ? The Barrister : Your vote is in splendid order, and I have no doubt you will use it in the right way. IF WOMEN HAD THE VOTE.

Referring to the persistence and volubility with which a claimant had argued his case, the Barrister remarked : This is the sort of thing that would happen if we had women voters. They would give us a treat. You would find nine out of every ten going through that performance. It would be too funny for words.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.

The revision for the polling districts of Whitley and Daresbury took place in the Sessions House at Dares- bury on Thursday. The Liberal agent supported a lodger claim in the parish of Preston-o'th-Hill, which was allowed. Trevor Moodield claimed for the second time as a lodger. Mr Cliffe again objected on the ground that he had not the sole use of a bedroom. The Barrister disallowed the vote. The ownership claim put in by the Liberals on behalf of Mr J W Hayward, J.P., in the parish of Whitley was allowed, and another for Mr A B Holt for Antrobus paresh was also sustained by Mr Cliffe. The lodger claims of Richard Frith and Fred Youd put forward by Mr Cliffe succeeded. The Rev W S Adams of Daresbury claimed a lodger vote in that parish, which was supported by both the party agents and allowed. This being the closing Court in the Knutsford Division, the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Revising Barrister for the manner in which he had presided over the various courts. Mr G Duckworth proposed a hearty vote of thanks to his honour and Mr H Cliffe in seconding said that whether the New Reform Bill now in the House of Commons became an Act and thereby abolished Revision Courts, or whether it did not, be should always have the pleasantest recollections of the patient and able way Mr Lloyd had gone through the various lists, and of the soundness and impartiality of his decisions in the cases brought into that court. In that sense, he (Mr Cliffe) regretted the contemplated abolition of the Courts as it had been a great pleasure and privilege to assist, along with Mr Duckworth, the Barrister in the annual revision. Mr Lloyd thanked the agents for their kindly refer- ences to himself, and said he greatly appreciated the valuable help of the two agents. Ile was particularly glad to see the friendly manner in which the cases were contested in the court. This was as it should be, and it made the work much easier for him. Mr Lloyd commences the revision of the lists in the Newtown Division of Montgomeryshire to-day (Saturday).

div.head: Death of Mr. H. S. Haddock.
div.p: Death of Mr. H. S. Haddock.

Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death, at the early age of 22 years, of Mr. Bernard Marsh Haddock (eldest son of the late Mr. T. C. Haddock and Mrs. Haddock, of Fearnhead, and nephew of Mr. W. Haddock, engineer of the Gas Department of the Corporation), who passed away at the Infirmary on Tuesday, following an operation for appendicitis. Mr. Haddock was engaged at the Gas Works at Long- ford as assistant to the engineer, and until Saturday was in r-ufficiently good health to be able to attend to his duties as usual. Not feeling well he went to spend the week-end with some friends, but became worse, and his removal to the Infirmary was found to be necessary. He was a keen football enthusiast, who was not content to watch others play, and he took part in his favourite game until a few days before his death. For one so young be had made a large circle of friends, and his death is deeply regretted. The funeral took place on Friday in the churchyard attached to Christ Church, Padgate.

div.head: BEECHAM'S PILLS.
div.p: BEECHAM'S PILLS.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
DIFFICULT CASE AT RUNCORN.

Elizabeth Randles, a young woman residing in Back High-street, Runcorn, was charged at Runcorn on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly. The girl was before the court a week ago and was remanded in order that her state of mind might be inquired into. Police-Constable Stokes said he found her on the evening of the 7th inst very drunk and behaving in an improper fashion in Victoria-road. The prisoner said she could not say how much she had had. In sentencing her to a month's imprisonment in the second division, Dr. WDougall said it would give the authorities the opportunity of finding out if drink or something else was the cause of her mental condition.

div.head: EASTBOURNE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE EASTBOURNE TRAGEDY.

Miss Florence Elizabeth Paler, the sole survivor of the Eastbourne tragedy, will leave Eastbourne in the course of the next few days for a place where she will be cared for. Her destination will be kept secret. The jurors at the Coroner's inquiry each received five shillings. They gave two shillings to the hospital, and three shillings to Florence Paler.

div.head: ESPONDENTS.
div.p: ESPONDENTS.
CHAS. DrKEs.—Owing to pressure on our space we have been compelled to hold your letter over till next week—En. "Ex."
Objectionable Picture Postcards.

Sir,—No doubt many of your readers will have noticed, along with myself, that the proprietor of a certain news and stationery shop in one of the main streets of cur town is at present exhibiting in his windows a large stock of exceedingly vulgar and suggestive p;cture post-cards. As far as I know, up to now the town has been remarkably free from this picture post-card nuisance, and if the person responsible in this case would pcuse to think of the harm he may be doing to the child-life of the town and also the slur he casts upon the town by having such an exhibition in the main streets, be would politely withdraw them. Perhaps he looks at it from a business point of view ; my own opinion is, that it may cause a crowd of a certain class to congregate round his windows, but I don't think it will increase his trade one atom—Your truly, AN OBSERVER.. September IStla, 1012,

div.head: Systematic Reading.
div.p: Systematic Reading.

Sir,—The National Home Reading Union, of which H.R.H. Princess Louise is president, and the Bishop of Hereford is chairman, is about to start its reading courses for the season. In its forthcoming" General Course," the subject of the " Administration of Charity" is included. While active workers in the Guild of Help will no doubt he taking up the course, there are probably many others who would like to study this or other subjects in a systematic way. Other topics included in the general course are "The open air," " Founders of the Empire," " The child at home, " " Dante," and " Words and their history." Special books are recommended and nine Magazines are issued monthly from October onwards, which give guidance in reading. The great advantage of the Horne Reading Union is its elasticity. People can read as much or little as they like according to leisure and inclination. I shall be glad to send full particu- lars to any who care to have them, if they will send me a po6tcard. —Yours faithfully, WILFRED J. ROWLAI.`TD. Winmarleigh Chambers, Warrington.

div.head: Paltry Progress.
div.p: Paltry Progress.

Sir,—Although " Labor Omnia Vincit " is in agree- ment with my remarks on working class productive co-operation I find myself unable to agree with his economics. I will not call his letter "a jumble" because he could crushingly reply "You're another," and we should make no progress. Come, let us reason together. First let me state my idea of economic laws in a few propositions. If each of these, or some of them, are accepted we can proceed step by step to build up a more complex theory of social evolution. If we disagree we know the exact 'mint whet e we part, and it will not be necessary for us to roam over the whole subject each trying to score a point over the other. Instead of using the terms" wages " and "prices " let us substitute the single term " standard subsist- ence "which means the amount of wealth which the workers consume. What the workers do not consume we will call sur42us value. We thus divide the whole ol the commodities produced kto two parts namely, earned and unearned. Let us see how these vary in the different industrial systems which have existed. In slavery it took about 80 per cent of the total -produce t) keep the slave. The remaining 20 was the share of the master. tinder the feudal system about GO per cent, was required for the living of the serf. Yet the serf had a better living than the slave. Although 40 per cent. of the total wealth was taken by the master class the remaining GO per cent, meant more wealth than the 80 per cent, received by the slave. The serf was a much more productive worker. He was more productive because he was more intelligent and because he was more intelligent he demanded and got a higher standard of subsistence than the slave. But 7w was worse off relatively. We come now to early capitalism, where we find that the workers received about 50 per cent, of their whole output. They are more intelligent (as a body) than the serfs and are capable of working complicated machinery. Their standard of subsistence is higher than the serf, but they are worse off comparatively. In modern capitalism educated workers are required, so the standard of subistence had to be raised, but it now represents only about .`;5 per cent. of the total product. From this we may deduce the law of the workers' standard of living. The standard of subsistence is forced down to the lowest level that the intelligence of the workers will permit. The serf would not live on the subsistence of the slave, while the wage-earner would not live on the subsistence of the serf. Modern workers would not live on what workers of 100 years ago lived on. This is manifested in various ways but the chief weapon has been their power of combination. Capitalists do not raise the standard until to resist raising it would involve greater loss to them. I find I am not able to finish this letter, so with your per- mission will continue it next week.—Yours truly. W. BAGITLEY. Stockham, Runcorn.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND LABOUR LAWS.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND LABOUR LAWS.
British Delegates' Good Work at Zurich.
[FROM THE "DAILY NEWS " CORRESPONDENT].

ZURICH, Sept. 14th. The International Association for Labour Legisla- tion (which is non-party and non-sectarian) has just concluded a notable congress here. Great Britain has for the first time sent two Labour delegates in the persons of Mr. Hodge, of the Iron and Steel Workers' Union, and Mr. Cox, of the Steel Smelters, whose presence after their work in London last June on the Hours of Labour Commission was rightly felt to be indispensable here. In conjunction with Mr. A. H. Crosfield they have rendered invalu- able service in framing the resolutions and influencing the decisions of the conference on the question of the eight hours' shift in continuous industries. This has been the outstandig question of the dele- gates' meeting. After complete discussion in com- mittee, in which the excessive hours worked in many Continental countries—notably in Germany—were set forth, it was wisely derided to take the cases of different " continuous industries " in the order of their simplicity and their strength—which luckily happened to coincide. The recommendation finally: agreed upon took the form of a request that the Swiss Federal Government would as soon as possible arrange an official confer- ence, having for its object the introduction of an eight- hours day for iron and steel workers ; that on the first favourable opportunity the introduction of a 56-hours week, with 24 hours rest at the week-end, for glasswork era should be considered ; and that the national sections should continue their work of investigation of other continuous industries, and industries in which employment exceeds ten hours per day, in order to prepare the way in these also for the introduction of an eight-hours day by international agreement. The discussions on the truck system and the place of fines and deductions in industrial life have also proved particularly lively and informing. In the end the proposed condemnation of fines and deductions was as complete and far-reaching as even the British delegates, who put the matter on the agenda paper, could desire

div.head: COUNTESS THROWN FROM HORSE'
div.p: COUNTESS THROWN FROM HORSE'

The Countess of Guilford broke her collar bone on Thursday morning as the result of her horse coming to grief at a fence while her ladyship was cub-buntin with the East Kent bounds. First aid was rendered by a Dover constable, and the countess was conveyed in a motor car to her Dover residence, Waldershare Park.

Mrs. Patrick Campbell, who is lying ill at her Kensington-square residence, London, was reported on Thursday night to be making satisfactory progress towards recovery. The well-known actress met with a motor accident a short while ago, and subsequently caught a cold.

div.head: OF THE BURNT OUT COACHES LITTERED WITH REMAINS OF
div.p: OF THE BURNT OUT COACHES LITTERED WITH REMAINS OF
ILL-PATED PASSENGERS' LUGGAGE.
FIFTEEN KILLED, FIFTY INJURED. LATEST PARTICULARS OF THE ACCIDENT.

An awful railway disaster, resulting in 15 deaths and injurie3 to about 50 persons, occurred on the London and North-Western Railway at Ditton Junction, near Widnes, at six o'clock on Tuesday evening. The train was coming from. Chester and was due at Lime-street, Liverpool at 6.27. It had callel at the principal stations on the I North Wales coast.

The accident happened on a sharp decline. The engine left the rails about 50 yards from the station and dashed into the buttress of the bridge. The carriages ran on, and the first two were reduced to matcbwood on the station platform, every passenger in them being killed. The fourth carriage, which stoppe d opposite the derailed engine became a roaring furnace, in which several passengers were burned to death before they could be rescued. -
Many ghastly and pathetic scenes were witnessed, especially at the burning coach, where the would-be rescuers were repeatedly driven back by the fire.

div.head: DEATH ROLL.
div.p: THE DEATH ROLL.

The death-roll is now officially stated to be 15. All the bodies have been identified, and information furnished by relatives at the formal opening of the inquest on Wednesday enables us to supply the following details : William B. Cordelle, aged 47, a director of Messrs Moussel Bros. and Co., furniture removers, of Liverpool, living at Victoria-road, The Brook, Liverpool. Albert and Agnes Robey, a married couple, of Cedlic House, Rainhill. Mr. Roby, aged 45, was a brass founder, and was returning with his wife from a holiday at Llandudno. His remains were identified by means of a gold watch. Mrs. Caroline Marshall, wife of a shipowner, of Earlscote, Moseley-hill, Liverpool. Miss Nesta Walmsley, of Green Park, Liverpool niece of the above, and also of Mr. Rigby Swift M.P. for St. Helens. She is the daughter of a Liverpool shipbroker. Mrs. Rees, of Glen Cairn, Abergele. Her husband is among the injured in Liverpool Infirmary. Miss Jane Owen, aged 4 21, of Chetwynd-street, Liverpool. She was returning for school from a holiday in North Wales with her parents, both of whom are seriously injured. Miss On en died in hospital. Mrs. Thomas, of Liverpool. Had been spending a holiday with two daughters at Almwicb, N. Wales. Her daughters returned by an early train but Mrs. Thomas went back for something, she had fo:gotten, with the result that sbe was a, passenger in the ill-fated train. Miss Margery Eleanor Lloyd,Logan-street Liverpool. Walter Samuel W. Garner, aged 31, an accountant, of 7, Laurels-road, St. Helens. Arthur Mason Poole, aged 35, bookkeeper, of The Drive, St. Helens. Miss Winifred Mary McArdle, aged 21, Ash Leigh, Sandown Park, W avertree, Liverpool. William Henry Sherwin. driver on the Great Central Railway, travelling as a passenger, living at Alvanley, Helsby, Cheshire. Robert Hughes, aged 41, driver of the ill-fated train. of Pensarn-cottages, Llandudno. Abraham Lunn the fireman, Bodbyfryd, Conway- road, Llandudno Junction.

div.head: DRIVER BLAMED.
div.p: THE DRIVER BLAMED.
STATEMENT BY AN OFFICIAL.

In spite of any theories which may be advanced as to the cause of the accident or of any attempts to fix the blame, it is still too early too form a just estimate of the causes contributing to the disastrous effect. A statement having an important bearing on the subject,however,was made onWednesday by Mr. W. Turnbull, district superintendent of the line. It appears from this that the official view of the accident is that the driver was at fault in travelling at an excessive speed. Mr. R. Turnbull, superintendent of the line, who had inspected the scene of the accident, said it was quite evident that the driver ought to have been going at a much slower pace than 50 miles an hour after he had received intimation at the distance signals a thousand yards away that he was being turned on to the slow line. Fifty miles was considered as a safe speed for the fast lines, but on the slow lines only 15 miles was allowed. The driver might have thought that he was still on the fast line, although

the signals he had passed had pointed to slow. Obviously he omitted to reduce the speed. It was not unusual for the train to be switched on to the slow line in this way. It had been done eleven times since the middle of August.

div.head: MIRACULOUS ESCAPE.
div.p: A MIRACULOUS ESCAPE.
WARRINGTON PASSENGERS' TERRIBLE ORDEAL.

Among the passengers in the front portion of the ill-fated train were., Mr. Frank E. Brown, of Sefton Park, Liverpool, his wife and fifteen months-old boy. Mr. and Mrs. Brown are well-known in Warrington where they resided before their marriage. Mr, Brown, who is a clerk in Parr's Bank, Liver- pool, is the son of Mr. George J. Brown, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath (a director of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, Warrington), and for many years was identified with Wycliffe Congregational Church,. being a member of the choir and an accept- able soloist. His wife is a daughter of Mr. J. Robinson, jeweller, Bridge-street. After spending a fortnight's holiday at Llandudno, Mr and Mrs Brown were return- ing home on Tuesday when the disaster to the train in which they were travelling plunged them into a terrible and nerve-trying ordeal Their escape was indeed a miraculous one, as is evidenced by the fact that three other occupants of the same compartment were killed. It was at the house of his father at Stockton Heath that Mr Brown was interviewed by an" Examiner" representa- tive on Wednesday morning and gave a thrilling account of his experiences. "As we approached Ditton" he said "I stood up to reach something off the rack. Suddenly I was flung against the carriage door. There was a crash in my ears almost like a roar of thunder, and then all was dark. I remem- bered nothing more for a time. When I came to myself I was almost smothered under the coach, which had completely over-turned. However, I was able to clamber out through tbe door at the top. I then saw my wife, who was pinned by the legs beneath the carriage. Two dead passengers were lying across her and she was soaked to the skin with blood from their injuries. Her face was terribly burned, through the explosion of gas in the train."

The awful suspense !undergme by Mr. Brown while endeavouring to free his wife from the wreckage in which she was imprisoned can be imagined. To add to the horror of the situation, the carriage had caught fire and the flames were getting perilously near. Little wonder that Mrs. Brown was impelled to cry out "I'm going mad." Happily the rescue was successfully carried out. "With the assistance of a navvy" said Mr. Brown "I managed to get her out in about half an hour, just as the fire was scorching her, and took her to the waiting room. There was no trace of our child and we had given him up, for lost, but a few minutes later a woman brought him along the platform and asked if he belonged to us." It was evident that the child had been thrown right out of the carriage and almost clear of the debris. Mr. Brown was carrying the little fellow in his arms when our repre- sentative called, and although there were bruises on his arms, legs and head, the child did not appear to have suffered any serious injury. Mr. Brown was rather badly cut about the head and legs, but at the time of the accident he was so pre-occupied with the fate of those dear to him that, until he reached StocktonHeath,he never realized that he himself might have suffered injury. Then he felt bloood trickling from the wounds on his head and found pieces of glass embedded in his hair. As stated above, Mrs. Brown sustained very severe burns about the face and the shock to her system was severe. After she had received medical attention at Ditton Station, Mr. Brown obtained a taxi- cab in which the three of them were driven to his father's house at Stockton Heath. Dr. Howard was summoned, and under his care MTS. Brown is progressing satisfactorily. Mr. and Mrs. Brown lost the whole of their luggage, which included articles of jewellery and a perambulator. "It was terrible" said Mr. Brown, summing up his experiences. " I can assure you I never want to see such sights again. There was a woman getting practically roasted
FRONT OF THE ENGINE AND THE BREACH MADE ;IN THE BU OF THE BRIDGE.

div.head: 'liE LINE JUST OUTSIDE DITTON STATION BRI Photos Bur
div.p: 'liE LINE JUST OUTSIDE DITTON STATION BRI Photos Bur

alive within two feet of me, and it was impossible to extricate her. The carriage itself was almost smashed to matchwood— there was little but the framework left. Three other occupants were killed. They were sitting on the side opposite to ourselves and would therefore have no chance of

escape." " Was there no warning at all that some- thing terrible was going to happen ? " asked the reporter. " No. There was at first a jolt, just like passing over points, and then I was dashed against the door and all was darkness." _ _

When it became known that Mr. and Mrs. Brown were passengers in the wrecked express, much concern was expressed by their many Warrington friends, who were later very greatly relieved to hear of their remarkable escape.

div.head: GAS-LIGHTING AND THE FIRE.
div.p: GAS-LIGHTING AND THE FIRE.

Three passengers who escaped almost without injury, although travelling in the second coach, which was completely smashed up, describe the engine as having left the line on the curve, where it was moving at a great speed. They appeai• to have freed them- selves from the carriage, through one of the windows, almost immediately, for they were in time to see the immediate results of the smash. According to their account, the carriages which were nearest the engine when the train came to a stop caught fire from the furnace. Probably the gas tanks used for the lighting of the coach lent dangerous fuel to the fire, once it had taken a good hold. A dense volume of steam escaping from the boiler prevented for some time any effort either to rescue the passengers from the coach or to deal with the fire.

div.head: JEWELLERY IN THE WRECKAGE.
div.p: JEWELLERY IN THE WRECKAGE.

The work of recovering the bodies and of treating the injured after their rescue from the train, which was carried out with the greatest dispatch in the first few hours after the accident, was so thoroughgoing and corn - pieta that no further signs of anybody that might by chance have been alive were dis- covered after eleven o'clock on Tuesday night. The work of clearing the railway has gone on continuously since the arrival of the first breakdown gang. A great deal of jewellery has been discovered, and various articles of personal luggage. It is thought possible, in view of the almost complete destruction of part of the train by fire. that some of the articles discovered may belong to victims of the wreck who are yet unknown because no other trace of them remains. Among the more gruesome dis- coveries made by the search parties on Tues- day were one or two fragments of bodies, and these, too, may belong to unknown passengers, though considering the exhaus- tive nature of the search this does not seem probable. The number of holidaymakers on the train was shown by the twisted frames of bicycles taken from the wreckage. Several cameras and holiday literature were to be seen, also a huge heap of oysters. Pathetic remnants included a pair of lady's gloves, a pair of child's boots, and portions of women's blouses In the waiting room mortuary was a high pile of clothing, among which was the jewellery, the value of which is said to be £5OO.

The Duchess of Westminster on Thursday laid the memorial stone of two new wings which form an important part of the great scheme for the renovation and extension of Chester General Infirmary 88 a memorial of King Edward. The duchess also received purses on behalf of the fund.

ANNUAL REPORT AND DIVIDEND.
enticism of the Insurance Act. -

The following is the report of the Directors of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, to the thirty-ninth annual meeting of shareholders, to he held at the company's office in Warrington, on September 30th. The Directors are: Messrs J S Harmood Banner, M.P., chairman, John .1 B7eckly, Richard Branoker, W P 'glands, Herbert S Blackly. The profits for the year ending June 31411, 1012, amount to £78,141 3s 10d, and the balance brought forward from last year is £13,359 3s 'Bd, together £91,500 7s 6d. An interim dividend at the rata of 6 per cent per annum on the first and second preference shares and 3 per cent per annum on the ordinary shares was paid in March last for the half-year ending December 31st, 1911, amounting to £19,633 15s. The Directors now recommend that a dividend be paid for the past half-year at the rate of 6 per cent per annum on the first and srcond preference shares, and 7 per cent per annum on the orainary shares, making with the interim dividend 5 per cent for the year, and a total distribution of £50,755 16s 81. The Directors further I recommend that £12.393 Ws 8d be added to the Reserve Fund, raising it to £352,500; that the sum of £19,528 3s 83, which represents the expenditure on capital arcount for the year, be written off, leaving a balance of £13,822 16s 63 to be careed fcrward. The Directors record, with deep regret, the loss which they and the Company have sustained by the death of their late deputy chairman, Mr W H Bleakly, who was one of the pioneers of the Lancashire iron trade, and who had been continuously connected with the works now carried on by the Company since the Iyear 1856. The members of the Board are now reduced to five in number,end the Directors consider it desirable 1 that additional appointments be made, and they recom- mend for election Mr John Bleckly, junior, and Captain Harmond Banner.

The Maypole Pit of the Moss Hall Coal Co., Ltd., is again in full operation and a large output of coal is being produced. The progress made at the works of the Partington Steel and Iron Co., Ltd., during the year has been satisfactory.. . .

Trade du-ring the year, both in coal and iron, has shown considerable improvement, but the stoppage of the works due to the prolonged strikes at the collieries, among the transport workers and other workmen, pre- vented the management from taking full advantage of a position otherwise satisfactory. The reduction of output, together with advanced wages entailed serious losses in some departments, and materially affected the profits of the year. The effects on the year's profits of the charges impoved for imperial taxes, local rates and workmen's compensation—over the amount of which the Directors can exercise no control—have of late assumed such large proportions that it is thought desirable that the shareholders should have the actual figures for the year placed on record, to enable them to appreciate how fa- their dividends are affected. They are as follows :
- - A Imperial Taxes Local Rates 13,548 5 10 Workmen's Compensation

£33,782 14 2 The short experience already obtained of the working of the National Insurance Act gives ample proof of the burdensome character of its provisions, and the Director Ware confident that they mill have the acquies- cence of the shareholders in recording the opinion that the Act not only contributes to the causes of unrest among the workmen, but is unjust in its incidence, and itnquitable and unfair in placing the whole cost, in the case of industrial companies, upon tbe ordinary shareholders. The effect of the Act upon the company's various undertakingr represents a new tax of over one per cent per annum upon the amount of the ordinary capital. In compliance with the Articles of Association, Mr W Peter itylands retires from the Board, for re-election. and is eligible
The auditors, Messrs Blease and Sons, also retire,and are eligible for re-eleciion.

div.p: THE PARTINGTON STEEL at IRON CO., LTD.

The following is the report of the directors of the Partington Steel and Iron Company, Limited, to the second annual general meeting of shareholders, to be held at the Company's office in Irlam, on September 30th, 1912. The Directors are : Ma.srs J S Harmood Banner, M.P., chairman, John J Bleckly, W Peter Rylands, Arthur H Cooper. In submitting their report and balance sheet for the year ending June 30th, 1912, the Directors have to record with deep regret the death of their late colleague, Mr William Henry Blackly. During the year substantial progress has been made with the new works, but unfavourable weather conditions have considerably delayed out-door operations during the last six months, CoKE-OvEN AND RESIDUAL BYE-PRODUCTS PLANTS.— Work is in a forward state in this department, and it is anticipated that a portion of the ovens may be ready to commence operations in January. BLAST FURNACE DEPARTMENT.IOSt of the steel structural work in connection with the furnaces and stoves is complete, and the brick work lining of the stoves, 4:c., well advanced. It is hoped that two blast furnaces will be ready to commence operations in the early part of next year. STEEL FURNACES AND ROLLING MILLS.—A consider- able proportion of the work connected with the foundations in these department is completed, and the execution of the contracts for engines and machinery is proceeding Satisfactorily. The auditors, Messrs Blease and Sons, retire, and offer themselves for re-election.
